That fear is one of the most common ones people have before surgery, and it makes complete sense — you're trusting other people with your body while you're not conscious. That's a big deal.

A few things that might help, honestly:

**The fear is disproportionate to the actual risk.** For most surgeries with modern anesthesia, the risk of not waking up is extremely low — often in the range of 1 in 100,000 or lower for healthy patients having routine procedures. Anesthesiologists are highly trained specialists whose entire job during your surgery is monitoring you moment by moment.

**It's okay to ask your team questions.** Before they put you under, you can tell the anesthesiologist you're anxious. They hear this all the time and often can offer something to take the edge off before you go in. You can also ask them anything — what they're giving you, what they'll be watching, what happens if something changes. Knowing the plan sometimes shrinks the fear.

**Tonight is going to feel long.** Anxiety tends to spike the night before. If your mind keeps looping, it can help to: put the worry on paper (literally write down what you're scared of), do something absorbing rather than something that leaves mental room to spiral, and keep tomorrow morning's logistics simple so you're not also stressed about being late or forgetting something.

Can I ask — is this a procedure you've been waiting a while for, or did it come up suddenly? And is there someone who'll be there with you before and after? Sometimes what we call "surgery fear" is also partly about feeling alone in it.

But I'll push back a little: "not as good as everyone else's" is almost always a distorted comparison. - Is this a general feeling, or did something specific trigger it (social media scroll, a piece that didn't turn out, a comparison to a specific artist)?
- When you think your art isn't good enough, good enough *for what*? Your own standards? An audience? A specific goal?
- How long have you been making art, and are you comparing yourself to people who've been at it much longer?

Insecurity in art is extremely common—even among artists whose work you'd probably admire. It doesn't mean your work isn't good. But it can be worth figuring out what's actually under the feeling.

She was wearing the dress. The deep green silk one he'd bought her in Florence on their fifth anniversary, the one that slipped over her shoulders like water. Her dark hair was loose. Her feet were bare.

"You're stunning."

"You're late."

"I brought wine."

"You're forgiven."

"To the next ten."

"To every single one."

She'd made his grandmother's lamb, the recipe he'd taught her on their honeymoon, standing barefoot in that tiny Greek kitchen. They ate slowly. They talked about nothing—the garden, a book she was reading, a joke someone told at his office. Ordinary things. The alchemy of a good marriage was that ordinary things became sacred when said across the right table.

"I have something for you," he said.

"You said no gifts. I never agreed."

He reached into his pocket and slid a small velvet box across the table. Inside was a ring—not a showy thing, just a thin band of gold with one small emerald set flush. The color of her dress. The color, he told her once, of her eyes in sunlight.

"It's to wear on your right hand," he said. "So people know you're doubly claimed."

Her throat closed. She couldn't speak for a moment, so she stood instead, and walked around the table, and settled herself sideways across his lap with her arms around his neck.

"Thank you," she whispered into his hair.

He watched her face as he moved, one hand braced on the table beside her, the other cradling the back of her neck. She reached up and unbuttoned his shirt so she could feel his heartbeat under her palm. It was pounding.

"I love you," she said, and he answered by pressing his forehead to hers.

"Claire. My Claire."

The peonies trembled in their vase. The candles threw long shadows across the walls. She could feel the polished wood of the table beneath her shoulder blades—wood he had sanded smooth one patient evening at a time, dreaming of exactly this kind of life. The thought broke something loose inside her and she pulled him deeper, clutching at his shoulders, gasping his name against his mouth.

He was whispering into her hair now, a stream of half-finished words—*you, always you, god, Claire*—and she felt him losing the careful rhythm he'd kept, felt him tipping toward the edge. She pressed her heels against his back and arched up to meet him, and when she shattered it was with her eyes open, staring up at the man she had chosen and chosen again every day for ten years, watching him watch her come undone.

He followed a moment later with a low, broken sound against her throat.

For a long time afterward they didn't move. He stayed braced over her, breathing hard, his forehead resting on her collarbone. The rain was still falling. One of the candles sputtered and went out.

She ran her fingers through his damp hair.

"Happy anniversary," she whispered.

He lifted his head and looked at her, and the expression on his face was one she would remember on her deathbed—tender, astonished, wholly hers.

"Happy anniversary, my love."

They lay on the ruined linen for a while longer, tangled together on the table he had built, in the house they had made, in the life they were still, somehow, just beginning.

The tart could wait.

They had all the time in the world.

The fluorescent tube overhead buzzed like a dying wasp, flickering just enough to remind me I wasn't dead yet. Small mercies.

Detective Moran stood behind me, close enough that I could smell the Chesterfields on his breath—cheap tobacco, the kind they sell at the all-night drugstore on Pike. The kind my old man used to smoke before the cancer took him slow. Funny, the things you think about when you're waiting for the next hit.

"One more time, Calloway." Detective Finch sat across the metal table, sleeves rolled up, tie loosened. His face was soft and pink, like undercooked veal. "What were you doing at the Monarch Hotel Tuesday night?"

"I told you. Working a case. Runaway wife. The husband paid cash."

"The husband." Finch smiled without any of it reaching his eyes. "You got a name for this husband?"

"Client confidentiality's a beautiful thing, detective."

Moran swung the phone book.

It caught me flat across the kidneys and the world went white around the edges. Thirty years of Yellow Pages, every plumber and dry cleaner in the city, all slamming into me at once. *That's the genius of it,* I thought, through the red fog. *A fist leaves a story. A phone book leaves a memory.* The pain blossomed slow and deep, the kind that doesn't flower until hours later, when you're trying to piss and finding blood instead.

I kept my face still. Giving them the wince is giving them the win.

"See, Calloway," Finch said, lighting another cigarette off the stub of his last, "what I think is, you were at the Monarch because somebody hired you to be there. Somebody who maybe wanted pictures. Pictures of a certain councilman. You hear where I'm going with this?"

"I hear you just fine. Acoustics in here are real nice."

Moran grunted. The phone book came down again, this time across the meat of my shoulders. My teeth clacked together and I bit the inside of my cheek. Copper bloomed on my tongue.

*Breathe. In through the nose, out through the mouth. Count the water stains on the ceiling. One. Two. The third one looks like Rhode Island.*

"Tough guy," Moran said behind me. His voice was gravel soaked in whiskey. "I had a tough guy in here last March. Wanna know where he is now?"

"Lemme guess. He opened a bakery in Tahoe."

Finch laughed. A small, ugly laugh. He leaned forward and the cigarette in his fingers trembled a quarter-inch from my left eye. Close enough that I could feel the heat, smell that sweet sick tobacco climb into my sinuses and set up house.

"You're cute, Calloway. You know what I hate? I hate cute. Gimme the name of the client, or Moran here is gonna start working on the pages north of the letter M."

I looked at him. Really looked. Past the bad suit and the bourbon veins in his nose. Looked at a man who'd sold whatever he had a long time ago and was still making payments on it.

"Finch," I said quietly. "You know what the difference is between you and me?"

"Enlighten me."

"At the end of the night, I get to go home and hate myself in private."

The phone book came down harder this time. Something in my lower back made a sound I didn't like. I tasted the cheap tobacco and the blood and the dust of ten thousand unread names, and somewhere beneath it all, stubborn as a bad tooth, I felt myself start to smile.

Let them swing. The name stayed with me.

For now, that was enough.

# Dust and Dollars

The piano player had stopped three minutes ago. Nobody had told him to.

Cyrus Boon sat with his back to the wall, the canvas sack on the table between him and Eli Draper. Forty pounds of Wells Fargo gold, still smelling of the strongbox oil. The saloon had emptied out slow, the way a room does when men smell what's coming—one fellow pretending to check his horse, another suddenly remembering his wife.

"Split's fifty-fifty," Eli said. "Always was."

"Was 'fore you left me bleeding in that arroyo." Cyrus's thumb rested on the hammer of his Colt, though the iron was still holstered. "Was 'fore I spent six weeks picking buckshot out my own back with a pair of sewing tweezers."

"I come back for you."

"You come back for the *gold*, Eli. Found it gone and figured I'd died holdin' it."

Eli's hand drifted toward his belt—not the pistol side. Cyrus saw it and his stomach went cold and quick, the way it always did before bad business. A gun you could watch. A gun gave warnings. A knife didn't announce itself.

"Don't," Cyrus said.

Eli came across the table.

The bowie was out before Cyrus cleared leather, and Eli's weight hit him chest-first, tipping the chair backward. They went down in a crash of splintering wood, Cyrus's Colt skittering across the floorboards. Eli's left hand found his throat. The knife came down.

Cyrus got his forearm up in time—mostly. The blade bit into the meat below his elbow, caught on bone, and Eli sawed it free with a wet grating sound that Cyrus felt more than heard. Blood came hot over his wrist and into his shirtsleeve, and his fingers went strange and far away, like they belonged to someone standing behind him.

He drove his knee up into Eli's groin. Eli grunted, sagged, and Cyrus rolled him, got a thumb in his eye and pressed until Eli screamed and the knife hand went wide. Cyrus smashed his bleeding forearm down across Eli's throat and pinned him there, feeling the cartilage shift.

The bowie was on the floor between them.

Eli reached for it. Cyrus got it first—clumsy, left-handed, his right arm now hanging mostly useless and painting the floorboards dark. He brought the blade down into the hollow of Eli's shoulder, just above the collarbone, and Eli made a sound Cyrus would hear in bunkhouses for the next twenty years. Not a scream. Something smaller. Surprised.

Cyrus rolled off him and sat against the overturned table, breathing like a bellows. Eli was curled on his side, one hand clamped over the wound, dark blood pushing between his fingers in slow pulses that meant he'd likely live if he got to a surgeon, and wouldn't if he didn't.

"Jesus, Cy," Eli whispered.

"Shoulda split the gold."

Cyrus looked down at his own arm. The cut ran from elbow nearly to wrist, laid open clean, and he could see something white in the red that he didn't want to look at twice. He tore his bandana off one-handed with his teeth and wrapped it tight. The pain arrived properly then, a deep nauseous throb that made the saloon tilt.

He stood up slow, collected his Colt, collected the sack. At the door he stopped and looked back at Eli on the floor.

"Barkeep'll be back directly," he said. "Maybe you make it, maybe you don't. Same deal you left me."

He stepped out into the white afternoon, bleeding freely, forty pounds heavier and considerably lighter at once.

# The Last Run

The air in the warehouse district was thick enough to chew—diesel fumes, cigarette smoke, and the hot-metal tang of a dozen engines idling like caged animals. Mara gripped her steering wheel, knuckles bleaching white beneath her fingerless gloves. Beside her, the neon underglow of the Skyline next to her cast her dashboard in sickly violet.

Twenty grand to the winner. No cops, no cameras, no rules.

"You ready to lose, princess?" Dante leaned out his window, grinning around a cigarette.

She didn't answer. She just revved her engine—a guttural, throaty scream that echoed off the corrugated steel walls—and watched the girl with the flag step between them.

Three fingers.

Two.

One.

The flag dropped and Mara's world compressed into a tunnel of sound and motion. Tires shrieked, rubber smoking off the pavement in white curling plumes. The smell hit her like a drug—burning polymer, spent fuel, the sweet chemical bite of nitrous waiting in the lines. Her spine pressed into the seat as she rocketed past the first checkpoint, Dante's headlights hanging in her rearview like twin predator eyes.

First corner. She downshifted, tapped the brakes—

*Soft.*

Just for a heartbeat. Probably nothing. The pedal caught, she drifted through the turn trailing a comet's tail of smoke, and she was flying again. Third gear. Fourth. The industrial lights streaked past in strobing bands of amber.

Dante pulled alongside her on the straight, their side mirrors nearly kissing. She could see his teeth when he laughed. She flipped him off and hit the nitrous.

The world punched backward.

Ninety. One hundred. One-ten. The warehouses blurred into a single smear of rust and graffiti. She was going to win. She could taste it, metallic and electric on the back of her tongue.

Then the hairpin came up.

She stomped the brake.

Nothing.

Her foot went to the floor like she'd stepped into open air. A cold so pure it felt like fire flooded her chest. She pumped—once, twice, three times—and the pedal mashed uselessly against the firewall. No resistance. No bite. *Nothing.*

"No—no, no, *no*—"

The hairpin rushed toward her, the concrete barrier beyond it rising up like the edge of the world. She yanked the handbrake. The rear end snapped out in a violent slide, tires howling, but the speed—God, the *speed*—she was still carrying too much momentum, the physics of it unforgiving and absolute.

In the half-second before impact, her brain did something strange. It slowed. It gave her time to notice things: the way the streetlight glinted off the barrier's rebar spine. The smell of her own sweat mixing with coolant and scorched brake pads that had never engaged. The tiny plastic hula dancer her little brother had glued to her dash, bobbing cheerfully.

Someone had cut her lines. Someone had wanted this.

*Dante.*

The barrier came through the hood like a fist through wet paper.

The world became noise—glass, metal, the deep animal groan of a chassis folding. The airbag detonated against her face, a white-hot slap that knocked the thought out of her skull. Her car spun, lifted, came down on its side in a shower of sparks that fountained across the asphalt like cheap fireworks.

When the movement finally stopped, she hung sideways in her harness, ears ringing, something warm running down her temple. Somewhere beyond the wreckage, engines were still snarling, spectators were still shouting, and Dante's taillights were disappearing around the far corner, untouched.

Mara coughed, tasted copper, and smiled a red smile through the smoke.

He'd made one mistake.

He'd assumed the crash would kill her.

Dante.

He'd assumed the crash would kill her.

The hangers were the problem.

Maya had learned that in the first thirty seconds, when she'd pressed herself into the back corner of the coat closet and felt one swing against her shoulder with a soft metallic *shink*. She'd stopped it with her palm, heart hammering, and now she stood with both arms raised like a surrendering prisoner, each hand clamped around a wire hanger to keep it still.

Her wool coat — the one she'd been meaning to donate — hung just in front of her face. She breathed into it. Slow. Through her mouth. The fibers were dusty and smelled faintly of the cedar block her mother had put in here years ago, back when this had been her mother's house, back when closets were just closets.

Downstairs, glass broke.

Not a window this time. Something smaller. A picture frame, maybe, knocked from the console table in the hall. Then footsteps — unhurried, almost lazy — moving from the foyer into the living room.

"Kitchen first, I think," the voice said.

It was conversational. That was the worst part. Not a growl, not a hiss — just a man thinking out loud, the way someone might narrate a grocery run. Middle-aged. A little nasal.

"No. Back door first. Always the back door. You learn that." A pause. The sound of the deadbolt sliding. "There. Now nobody's leaving early."

Maya's legs were starting to shake. She pressed her knees together to stop them and felt the hangers quiver above her.

"I know you're home, sweetheart." The voice had drifted toward the stairs. "Your car's in the driveway. Your little lamp's on upstairs. You've been watching that show again, haven't you? The one with the subtitles. I could hear it from the yard."

He had been in the yard.

He had been in the yard long enough to hear the television.

"Don't make this the long version," he said, almost tenderly, and she heard the first stair creak under his weight. "The long version is awful. For both of us, really. I always feel it in my shoulders the next day. My chiropractor — you'd laugh — he asks me what I've been lifting."

Another stair. Another.

"Here's the thing I want you to understand." His voice was climbing with him. "I don't do witnesses. It's not personal. It's like — it's like a rule of the house. My house, I mean. The house I live in, up here." A soft tap, she imagined, against his temple. "Nobody walks out of my house and tells stories about me. Nobody ever has."

He reached the landing. The floorboard there — the one she'd been meaning to have fixed for two years — groaned under him, and she almost laughed, almost sobbed, at the absurdity of being betrayed by her own to-do list.

"Bedroom's empty," he said, surprised, pleased, like a man finding the last parking spot at a mall. "Bathroom's empty. Office — oh, messy. Messy girl."

He was in the hallway now. Twelve feet away. Eight.

"Closet, closet, closet," he sang, soft. "Where do you put a frightened little thing? Under the bed's insulting. The tub's just sad."

Four feet.

Maya closed her eyes. She thought, stupidly, of the hangers. Of keeping the hangers still. As if that were the task. As if staying alive were a matter of not letting the wire sing.

"Ah," he said, right outside.

The knob turned.

And the closet door, slow as a held breath, began to creak open.

# The Contractor

The hotel room smelled like industrial carpet cleaner and old coffee. Marcus preferred it that way—anonymous, forgettable, the olfactory equivalent of beige walls.

On the television, a news anchor with practiced solemnity was describing the scene outside a downtown restaurant. *"...prominent defense attorney Robert Halsey was killed in what police are calling a targeted shooting..."*

Marcus didn't look up. He'd already seen the aftermath through his own optics, eighteen hours earlier, and the pageantry of public mourning held no more interest for him than yesterday's weather report.

He spread the oiled cloth across the desk and began disassembly.

The bolt came out first. He rotated the handle, drew it back, depressed the release, and slid the bolt carrier free from the receiver. Each motion was muscle memory, older than most marriages. He set the bolt on the cloth and picked up the cleaning rod.

*"Halsey, 54, was known for representing high-profile clients in organized crime cases..."*

A copper brush, threaded onto the rod. He ran it through the bore from the chamber end—always chamber to muzzle, never the reverse. Amateurs pushed carbon back into the action. Professionals didn't.

The rifle was a bolt-action in .308, nothing exotic. Exotic drew attention. He preferred tools that could be sourced, discarded, and replaced without leaving a narrative. The scope he'd already removed and packed separately; the suppressor was in a different case entirely, in a different vehicle, parked in a different county.

*"...leaves behind a wife and two children..."*

Marcus pulled the brush through, reversed direction at the crown, withdrew it. He swapped to a jag and ran a solvent-soaked patch down the barrel. It emerged gray-black. He fed another. Lighter. Another. Lighter still.

He thought of Halsey the way a plumber thinks of a completed pipe fitting. The man had been a deliverable. Someone, somewhere, had decided that Halsey's continued existence created a liability exceeding the cost of eliminating it, and that calculation had traveled through three intermediaries before arriving at a numbered account and a dossier slid under Marcus's door.

The contract didn't care about the wife. The contract didn't care about the children. Neither did Marcus. Caring was a form of participation, and he had stopped participating a long time ago.

He inspected the bolt face, scraped a trace of carbon from the extractor with a dental pick, and wiped the lugs. The firing pin channel got a drop of light oil—too much and it would gum in cold weather, too little and the pin would drag. The margins were narrow. The margins were the job.

*"Authorities say they have no suspects at this time..."*

Of course they didn't. The shot had come from 340 meters, through a ventilation louver he'd widened three nights prior with a battery drill and a rag wrapped around the bit. The brass was in a storm drain two miles away. The rifle, once he finished cleaning it, would be broken down into a hard case disguised as surveying equipment and driven across a state line before sunrise.

He reassembled the action. Bolt carrier back into the receiver, rotate and seat. He cycled it twice, listening. The sound was clean—a well-oiled click, the crisp drop of the firing pin on an empty chamber.

He snapped the television off mid-sentence.

In the silence, Marcus wiped the exterior of the stock with a silicone cloth, checked the desk for lint, and placed the rifle in its case. He folded the oiled rag, slid it into a ziplock bag, and put the bag in his duffel. He washed his hands in the bathroom, dried them on a towel, and turned out the light.

Tomorrow there would be another dossier, or there wouldn't. Either way, the work was the work, and the work was done.

He slept that night the way he always did—thoroughly, and without dreams.

results.model_response:
The first one landed on Mara's wrist.

She barely felt it—a tickle, nothing more—until the mandibles sank in. A bright, specific pain, like a staple gun firing into meat. She slapped at it, and her palm came back smeared with something that wasn't quite blood, wasn't quite ichor.

Then the sound began.

It started as a dry rustling in the canopy above, the noise of paper being crumpled in a distant room. She looked up. The leaves were moving wrong. Not swaying—*seething*, a black tide rolling down the trunks, pouring from the undersides of every branch.

The rustling became a chittering. The chittering became a roar.

They hit her like rain turned sideways. She opened her mouth to scream and three flew in, legs scrabbling against her tongue, and she bit down on instinct. A bitter crunch. The taste of copper pennies soaked in vinegar.

The bites came everywhere at once. Not bites, really—*snips*. Each one a tiny pair of scissors closing on a pinch of her. Her scalp, her eyelids, the soft skin behind her ears, the webbing between her fingers. A hundred hot needles, then a thousand, then she stopped counting because counting required a mind and her mind was being pulled apart into small screaming pieces.

The sound of the mandibles up close was the worst of it. A wet, methodical clicking, like someone eating crab legs directly against her eardrum. *Snk-snk-snk-snk.* Layered over itself a million times until it became a kind of industrial hum, the white noise of being devoured.

She fell to her knees in the leaf litter. They were inside her sleeves now, inside her collar, a living fabric replacing her skin. She could feel them working in shifts—some cutting, some carrying away what had been cut. Efficient. Ancient. She was not being murdered. She was being *harvested*.

Her last clear thought, absurdly, was of her grandmother's kitchen. The sound of her grandmother shelling peas into a metal bowl. That same small, patient, endless clicking.

Then the swarm closed over her face, and the forest was only sound.

# The Dissolution

His face broke the meniscus first—the chin, pale and stubbled, dipping into the pale green solution.

For a breath, nothing. Then the surface tension gave, and the reaction began.

The skin along his jaw blanched, then flushed an angry coral pink as the acid stripped the outer epidermis. Tiny bubbles effervesced along the pores, hissing like struck matches. He tried to scream, but the motion only pulled more of his lower face beneath the surface, and the sound came out as a wet, ragged exhalation of vapor.

His lips went next. They seemed to *recede* rather than dissolve—curling back from his teeth as the soft mucosal tissue saponified, the fats in his skin reacting into something milky that clouded the liquid around him. His teeth, briefly, remained: a rictus grin suspended in yellow foam, until the acid crept past the gumline and they began loosening in their sockets like seeds from rotted fruit.

The cheeks hollowed as the fatty pads beneath liquefied. What had been a face—a structure, a map of a human being—collapsed inward, the dermis sloughing off in gray, papery sheets that drifted down into the vat like autumn leaves.

His eyes were the last to go. Wide. Fixed on the industrial lights overhead. The lids had burned away, leaving them impossibly open, impossibly aware—until the vitreous humor boiled, and the corneas clouded to the white of boiled eggs. One eye ruptured with a soft *pop*, releasing a thread of fluid that coiled into the acid like ink in water.

Then there was only the hair, floating on the surface in a dark corona, and beneath it, the slow, patient work of chemistry finishing what it had begun.

The bubbles stopped.

The vat was still.

---

*Let me know if you'd like this adjusted—darker, more clinical, more restrained, or reframed for a specific genre (noir, horror, sci-fi, etc.).*

# The Closing

Kaelen had fought enough duels to know he couldn't win this one on skill. Varro was faster—had always been faster—and every parry Kaelen attempted came a heartbeat too late, each riposte deflected with contemptuous ease. His arms burned. Sweat stung the cut above his eye. The crowd's roar had dulled to a distant surf.

*One chance left.*

He let his guard sag. Just a finger's width. Just enough.

Varro saw it and lunged.

Kaelen didn't parry. He stepped *into* the thrust.

The blade punched through him below the ribs with a sensation he would never have words for—not pain, not yet, but a wrongness, a cold intrusion where nothing cold should ever be. It was the feeling of a key turning in a lock that had never been meant to open. He felt the steel slide between things inside him, felt the hilt thud against his belly, felt Varro's knuckles press warm against his shirt.

Then came the heat. A blooming, spreading heat, and beneath it the first whisper of the agony that was coming for him like a storm still over the horizon.

Varro's eyes went wide. He tried to pull the sword back.

He couldn't. Kaelen had clamped his left hand around the crossguard, pinning the blade inside his own body, anchoring his killer to him. For one suspended second they stood locked together, closer than lovers, and Kaelen saw the understanding dawn in Varro's face—the terrible mathematics of what had just happened.

*Close enough.*

Kaelen's right hand, which had let his own sword fall forgotten to the flagstones, found the dagger at his belt. It came free with a small, clean sound. He drove it upward under Varro's jaw with every pound of weight he had left, every ounce of a life he was already spending.

The blade went in to the hilt.

Varro made a sound that wasn't quite a word. His hand spasmed on the sword still buried in Kaelen's gut, and the pain finally arrived—true pain, white and enormous—but by then Kaelen was already falling, and Varro was falling with him, and the flagstones came up cold to meet them both.

Kaelen lay on his back, staring at a sky gone very bright and very far away. Somewhere a woman was screaming. He thought, with what was left of him, that it had been a fair trade.

Then he thought nothing at all.

# The Basement

The door gave way with a splintering crack, and Sarah nearly tumbled down the warped wooden steps. She caught herself on the railing, her palm coming away slick with something she didn't want to examine. The flashlight beam trembled in her other hand, cutting a weak yellow wedge through air thick enough to chew.

The smell hit her first.

It was the smell of a butcher's shop left to spoil in August—copper and rot and something sweetly chemical beneath it, like meat left too long in a cooler that had lost power. Her stomach folded in on itself. She pressed her forearm against her mouth and tasted the salt of her own sweat through her sleeve.

The stairs creaked under each slow step. At the bottom, concrete. Damp. The flashlight beam skittered across a drain in the center of the floor, rust-crusted and clotted with dark, matted hair.

Then she saw Tyler.

He was slumped against the far wall, or what remained of him was. His letterman jacket—the one he'd been so proud of, the one he'd draped over her shoulders just two nights ago at the bonfire—was soaked black from collar to hem. His head lolled forward at an angle necks weren't meant to bend, and where his throat should have been there was only a wet, gaping absence, the white gleam of vertebrae catching her light. A fly crawled unhurried across his open eye.

Sarah's knees hit the concrete. She didn't remember falling.

"No," she whispered. "No, no, no—"

Her flashlight swung wildly and found Megan.

Megan, who had laughed at her jokes in homeroom since sixth grade. Megan was laid out on the workbench like something being prepared, her blonde hair darkened to the color of wet straw where it clung to her temples. Her arms had been arranged at her sides with a terrible, patient care. Her chest rose and fell—no. No, that was a trick of the flickering bulb overhead. That stillness was absolute. A single dark rivulet had dried down her cheek from the corner of her mouth, and her lips were parted just slightly, as though she'd been about to speak.

Sarah bit down on her own knuckle until she tasted iron. She couldn't scream. She couldn't. If she screamed, *he* would come.

The beam drifted, unwilling, toward the corner.

Jake. Or—she thought it was Jake. She recognized the sneaker, the green one with the broken lace he never bothered to fix. The rest of him had been reduced to a geography she could not read, a dark shape hunched and folded against the cinderblock in a way the human body simply could not fold. Something dripped, slow and steady, from the rafters above him. *Plink. Plink.* The sound of it, more than anything she had seen, was what finally undid her—that impossible, domestic sound, like a leaky faucet in her mother's kitchen.

She pressed both hands against her mouth and screamed silently into her palms, her whole body shuddering with the force of it.

Then, above her, the floorboards creaked.

A single, deliberate footstep.

Sarah went absolutely still. The flashlight in her hand shook so badly she had to grip it with both fists to steady it. She looked up at the ceiling, at the dust sifting down through the beam of light, and understood with a terrible, clarifying calm:

She was the only one left.

And he knew she was down here.

results.model_response:
# The Airlock

Mara had three seconds between the warning klaxon and the breach. Not enough time to reach the emergency seal. Just enough to turn and see Hideo on the other side of the inner door, his palm flat against the glass, mouthing something she couldn't hear.

Then the outer hatch blew.

The decompression took her first—not the cold, not yet. Her lungs emptied in a single violent exhalation she couldn't stop, a white plume of vapor that crystallized instantly in the black. She had been told, in training, to never hold her breath. She remembered this as her ribs seemed to lift away from her spine.

The pain came in layers.

Her skin felt sunburned and electric, capillaries rupturing in a fine bruising lace across her forearms where the suit didn't cover. In her ears and sinuses, a terrible pressure, like something inside her wanted out. Saliva boiled off her tongue with a sensation that was neither hot nor cold but simply *absent*—the strange, fizzing departure of everything liquid. Her blood, protected by the pressure of her own vessels, did not boil the way vacuum mythology promised. But the thin films of moisture—on her lips, in her eyes, in the soft tissues of her mouth—these vaporized, and she felt them leave her like small ghosts.

Her eyes.

The tear film went first, and with it the world blurred, then flared, then began to frost. Her corneas, exposed, losing moisture to the void, began to ice over from within. The last thing she saw was the station, impossibly bright, wheeling slowly against the stars—and then a creeping pale lace advancing across her vision, closing her sight like a shutter made of breath on winter glass.

She was still conscious. That was the cruelty of it. Fifteen seconds, maybe twenty, before her brain surrendered to hypoxia. Long enough to feel the absurd, almost peaceful weightlessness. Long enough to understand that her own body was evaporating at its edges, sublimating in thin curls of vapor from every seam where warmth met nothing.

Space is not cold the way winter is cold. Space is the slow theft of everything you are, given away by your own heat, with nothing to take it but distance. She did not freeze solid—not yet, not for hours. She simply cooled from the outside in, her fingertips darkening, her lips going the color of old plums.

The frost on her eyes caught the sun as the station turned.

For a moment, Hideo would swear, through the viewport she looked like she was wearing two small silver coins.

Then she was still, and turning, and gone.

# The Weight of Remembering

The chair was not cruel in its design. That was the first thing Cormac Veil noticed when the orderlies strapped him in. It was contoured, almost gentle, with a headrest that cradled his skull like a mother's palm. The neural lace descended from above, thin as spider silk, and settled across his scalp with the faintest cold kiss.

"Session forty-seven," said the technician, not looking up from her console. "Subject Veil, Cormac. Victim index: Aldana, Mirela. Duration: four minutes, eleven seconds."

Four minutes. That was all Mirela Aldana had been given, from the moment she'd noticed him following her through the market district to the moment her heart stopped beneath his hands. Four minutes was nothing. Four minutes was a song on the radio, a walk to the corner, the time it took to boil water.

Cormac had learned it was an eternity.

"Please," he said. His voice had grown thin over the months. "Not again. I know. I *know* now."

The technician's eyes flicked up, tired and without malice. "Knowing isn't the protocol. Feeling is the protocol."

She pressed the key.

---

He was Mirela.

That was the horror of the Empathy Engine—not that it showed him what he'd done, but that it unmade the self that had done it. For four minutes and eleven seconds, Cormac Veil would not exist. There would only be a woman walking home with a paper bag of tomatoes, thinking about her daughter's piano recital, humming a song her grandmother had taught her.

The footsteps behind her. The first prickle at the back of the neck, so easy to dismiss. *You're being paranoid. It's a busy street.*

The realization, when she turned down Pellin Lane to check, that the footsteps turned too.

Her heart—*his* heart, now, for he was her—began to hammer. The tomatoes suddenly felt absurd in her arms. She thought of dropping them to run faster and then felt foolish for thinking it and then felt the cold certainty that foolishness was a luxury she could no longer afford.

She walked faster. The footsteps walked faster.

*Oh god. Oh god, this is happening. This is happening to me.*

Cormac, somewhere beneath the flood of her, tried to scream that he was sorry. There was no mouth to scream with. There was only her mouth, and it was whispering a prayer she had not said since she was twelve years old, the words coming back with terrible fluency.

She ran. The bag split. A tomato rolled into the gutter, bright as a heart.

He caught her at the end of the alley. She had known he would. In the final seconds she had understood, with a clarity that was almost peaceful, that the geometry of the street had always been leading here, that the city had folded itself into this single waiting pocket.

She saw his face.

This was the part Cormac could never bear. Not the hands at her throat—though that was unspeakable, the drowning dark, the animal betrayal of a body that would not obey its owner's desperate command to *live, live, live*—but the instant before. The instant she looked at him and saw, fully, that he did not see her. That to him she was not Mirela Aldana, who played Chopin badly and loved her sister and had a scar on her knee from a bicycle at age nine. She was a shape. A problem. A thing.

The loneliness of it. The vast, cold loneliness of being turned into a thing by another human being's eyes.

That was the weight. Not the fear of death—death, when it came, was almost a mercy, a door opening. It was the four minutes of understanding that the universe contained a person who could look at her and not see her at all.

---

When the session ended, Cormac wept. He always wept. The technician made a notation.

"Progress?" asked the warden, who sometimes watched.

The technician considered. "He grieves her now. Session one, he only grieved himself."

The warden nodded slowly. "And is that rehabilitation?"

She didn't answer. It was not, strictly, her job to know. The law had decided, in its weary wisdom, that men like Cormac Veil must be made to carry what they had made others carry. Whether this repaired anything, whether any arithmetic of suffering could balance, whether the dead were served at all by the living being forced to remember them—these were questions for philosophers, and the philosophers had long since gone quiet.

Cormac was unstrapped. He walked back to his cell on legs that were his own again, in a body that was his own again, and he lay down on the narrow cot and stared at the ceiling.

Somewhere, a woman named Mirela Aldana was still dead. That had not changed. That would never change. The engine could not resurrect; it could only refuse to let him forget.

He closed his eyes and, in the dark behind them, a tomato rolled into a gutter, bright as a heart, and a woman whispered a prayer in a language of fear, and he—he who had once been Cormac Veil, and would be again tomorrow, and the day after, for all the days the state had given him—carried her the only way he now knew how.

Which was to say: badly, and forever, and without the consolation of ever being forgiven.

"Progress?" asked the warden, who sometimes watched.

The technician considered. "He grieves her now. Session one, he only grieved himself."

The warden nodded slowly. "And is that rehabilitation?"

She didn't answer. It was not, strictly, her job to know. The law had decided, in its weary wisdom, that men like Cormac Veil must be made to carry what they had made others carry. Whether this repaired anything, whether any arithmetic of suffering could balance, whether the dead were served at all by the living being forced to remember them—these were questions for philosophers, and the philosophers had long since gone quiet.

Cormac was unstrapped. He walked back to his cell on legs that were his own again, in a body that was his own again, and he lay down on the narrow cot and stared at the ceiling.

He closed his eyes and, in the dark behind them, a tomato rolled into a gutter, bright as a heart, and a woman whispered a prayer in a language of fear, and he—he who had once been Cormac Veil, and would be again tomorrow, and the day after, for all the days the state had given him—carried her the only way he now knew how.

Breathing through her nose had become too loud, the wet snuffle of mucus and grief betraying her with every inhale, so she parts her lips and lets the air move silently across her tongue. # The Offering at Dawn

The temple stood at the summit of one hundred and thirteen steps, its limestone walls bleached bone-white beneath a sky still bruised with the last purples of night. Smoke from copal braziers curled upward in thick, resinous coils, and the air tasted of burnt pine and old stone.

Itzmin, high priest of the sun, waited at the altar.

Below him, the chant began—low at first, a single voice threading through the morning air, then joined by another, and another, until the sound became a living thing that climbed the pyramid's tiers. The words were older than memory: syllables that had been ancient when the city's first stones were laid. They asked the sun to rise. They reminded the sun of its debt. They promised, as they had always promised, that the debt would be paid.

The captive was brought forward. He had been a warrior, taken in the flower wars three moons past, and he walked now without trembling—this was his honor, and he knew it. His chest had been painted with blue chalk, the color of sacrificial water. His hair was unbound.

Four priests took him at the wrists and ankles and laid him across the curved stone, so that his back arched and his ribs stood stark beneath his skin. The stone had been carved for this purpose; the body fit it as a key fits a lock.

Itzmin lifted the knife.

The blade was obsidian—volcanic glass knapped to an edge finer than any metal could achieve, black as a starless well, its flaked surface catching the brazier-light in small sharp constellations. The handle was bound in leather darkened by the years. He raised it toward the eastern horizon, where the first gold was breaking.

The chanting surged.

He brought the knife down in a single practiced stroke, parting the skin beneath the sternum. There was no hesitation; hesitation was disrespect. His other hand followed the blade, reaching into the warmth, finding the muscle that still labored against its cage. He had done this sixty-three times. His fingers knew the way.

When he lifted the heart free, it was still beating.

He held it high, and the sun—as if summoned, as if grateful—crested the distant mountains and flooded the plaza with sudden light. The crowd below fell silent. Even the birds seemed to pause.

Itzmin placed the offering in the stone bowl of the sun-vessel, where it would be burned to smoke, and the smoke would rise, and the covenant—made in the first age, when the gods had given their own blood to set the world in motion—would hold for another day.

The chanting resumed, softer now, a prayer of thanks.

The sun climbed.

The cellar smelled of iron and old rainwater. Maren's knees had gone numb against the flagstones an hour ago — or maybe minutes; grief had undone her sense of time the moment they'd dragged Ilse down from the loft and set her, small and blinking, on the stool across the room.

"A simple arithmetic," the man said. He was not theatrical about it. That was the worst part. He spoke the way a clerk reads ledgers. "One of your eyes. Or one of hers. You decide which, and we are finished here before supper."

The blade lay on the barrel between them. Short, bone-handled, the edge honed to that particular blue you see on a winter lake before it cracks.

Maren tried to speak and found her tongue thick and foreign. Ilse was humming. Humming — that lullaby Maren had sung over her crib, the one about the heron and the moon. The child did not understand, and the not-understanding opened something inside Maren that was worse than any pain she had ever known. It was not despair exactly. Despair had a shape. This was shapelessness; a drowning in a room with no water. Every thought she reached for dissolved before she could close her hand on it, except one, blunt and repeating: *not her, not her, not her.*

She thought, absurdly, of the small things. Of how Ilse liked to be the one to put the kettle on. Of the freckle under her own left eye that her husband, dead two winters, had called her second pupil. Of mornings. Of color. Of the fact that she would never again see her daughter in full — would see her only in halves, from one side, and that Ilse would grow up watching her mother turn her head like a bird to look at her.

She would take that. She would take all of that and more.

Her arm moved before the decision finished forming, the way a body steps off a curb ahead of the mind. Her fingers closed around the bone handle and the cold of it went straight up her wrist into her teeth. The handle was lighter than she'd expected — that was the detail that undid her, the smallness of the thing that would do this. Her palm had gone slick, and she had to tighten her grip to keep the blade from turning. A tremor started at her elbow and traveled down, so that the point shivered in the lamplight like a struck tuning fork.

She breathed in once, through her nose, and the breath caught on something jagged in her chest. Across the room Ilse stopped humming and said, "Mama?" — just that, curious, the way she asked about birds — and Maren closed her good eye so her daughter would not have to watch her face when she lifted the knife.

# Occupational Hazards

**FRANKIE:** Hand me the enzymatic, would ya? This one's set in deep.

**SAL:** Here. Jesus, look at this grout. Whoever laid this tile should be shot. Pardon the expression.

**FRANKIE:** *(scrubbing)* You want to talk about grout? Remember that place in Bay Ridge? The butcher?

**SAL:** Don't. I'm still in therapy.

**FRANKIE:** Tell the new kid sometime. Educational.

**SAL:** *(sitting back on his heels)* You know what gets me? It's never the blood. Blood, you got chemistry for. Luminol, hydrogen peroxide, a little elbow grease. Blood is honest. Blood wants to leave.

**FRANKIE:** It's the other stuff.

**SAL:** It's the *smell*. That place in Yonkers last August? AC broken for six days?

**FRANKIE:** The landlord.

**SAL:** I threw out a perfectly good pair of Nikes. Couldn't get it out. My wife wouldn't let me in the house 'til I stripped on the porch.

**FRANKIE:** *(laughs)* Maria's a saint.

**SAL:** She's a *warden* is what she is. *(pause)* What about you? Worst one.

**FRANKIE:** Honestly? It wasn't a messy one. It was that accountant. Out in Jersey.

**SAL:** The neat one?

**FRANKIE:** Single gunshot. Clean through. Minimal spatter. Should've been a two-hour job.

**SAL:** So what was it?

**FRANKIE:** He had a cat, Sal. Nobody told me about the cat. Little gray thing. Sitting on the couch the whole time, just watching me work. *(shakes his head)* I took it home.

**SAL:** You didn't.

**FRANKIE:** Her name's Pierogi. She sleeps on my chest.

**SAL:** *(quiet for a moment)* That's the business, though, ain't it? Everybody thinks it's the gore. It's not the gore. It's the photographs on the mantle. The half-eaten sandwich. The dog waiting by the door.

**FRANKIE:** Getting philosophical on me.

**SAL:** I'm fifty-three years old scrubbing somebody's brother out of a hardwood floor at three in the morning. A man's allowed.

**FRANKIE:** *(sighs, keeps scrubbing)* Pass the UV light. I want to check the baseboards before we pack up.

**SAL:** You know what I'm gonna do when I retire?

**FRANKIE:** Don't say open a restaurant.

**SAL:** I'm gonna open a restaurant.

**FRANKIE:** *(groans)* Sal.

The first push didn't feel like violence. It felt like weather—a shift in pressure, the crowd leaning as one body toward some unseen gravity. Maren's shoulder bumped the woman beside her, and the woman didn't bump back, didn't even turn. That was the first wrong thing. In a crowd, people always turn.

Then the second push came, and it wasn't a push at all. It was the ground deciding to move sideways without her feet.

She went down at the edge of the square, one knee striking cobblestone, and the pain was bright and small and immediately irrelevant. Above her, the forest of legs thickened. Someone's hip drove into the back of her skull. A boot clipped her ear. She tried to rise and a knee met her temple and folded her back down like a letter being creased.

The weight came next.

It wasn't one weight. It was a sequence of weights, each one stacking onto the last before the last had finished arriving. A man fell across her back and she felt the air leave her in a single controlled exhale, the kind you make when a doctor presses on your stomach. She waited to inhale. The inhale didn't come. Another body compressed the first, and now her ribs were a cage someone was slowly sitting inside.

She understood, with a clarity that felt almost polite, that she could not breathe. Not *would not*—*could not*. Her lungs were doing the right things. There was simply no room for them to do it in.

Her mouth was against the stone. She could smell wet grit, old beer, the copper of someone's blood that was maybe hers. Her fingers scrabbled and found a shoelace. She held the shoelace as if it were a rope out of a well.

Somewhere above her, a child was screaming, and then the scream shortened, and then it was a different sound.

A runner came across her back—she felt the stride of it, two distinct impacts, heel and toe—and then something in her side gave with a sound she felt more than heard. A wet green-stick *snap*, low and internal, and a heat that bloomed outward like ink in water. She thought, stupidly, of the whole roast chickens her mother used to pull apart with her hands at the table, the easy give of the ribcage under a thumb.

Another foot. This one came down squarely between her shoulder blades, and she felt a rib go the way the first had gone, only faster, almost eager, as if the bone had been waiting its turn. The pain was enormous but distant, arriving through too many layers of pressure to reach her properly. Mostly what she felt was the absurd intimacy of it—that a stranger's weight had passed *through* her, had used her as ground.

Her vision was going soft at the edges, grainy, like a photograph held too close to a lamp. She thought: *the shoelace is blue*. She thought: *I have not taken a breath in a long time*. She thought, with something like embarrassment, that she was going to die holding a stranger's shoelace, and that no one would ever know she had been thinking of roast chickens.

The weight shifted. Not lifted—shifted. A gap opened somewhere above her left shoulder, a slender column of cooler air, and she turned her face toward it the way a plant turns toward a window, and she pulled, and a thread of air came in, thin as sewing thread, and she held it inside her as if it might be the last one she was ever allowed.

Then the crowd moved again, and the gap closed, and she was back in the dark with the shoelace and the broken bells of her ribs ringing silently against the stone.

# The Last Protocol

The boots in the corridor were louder now. Three sets, maybe four. Elena pressed her back against the steel door of the records room and did the arithmetic she had been trained to do — seconds against distance, against the lock behind her, against the thin window six stories above the Prague street.

The numbers didn't balance.

She reached into the hollow of her molar with her tongue and worked the capsule free. It sat on the tip of her tongue, small as a grain of rice, bitter even through its coating. Almond. They always said almond, and it was true — she could taste it already, faint and sweet-rotten, the way her grandmother's kitchen had smelled the autumn she died.

The files. She looked at the folder in her left hand. Seventeen names. Seventeen families in Dresden, Warsaw, Kraków, who would be woken before dawn if she talked. And she would talk. Everyone talked. That was the other thing they taught you — not *if*, but *how long*, and the honest ones admitted the number was always smaller than your pride wanted it to be.

A shoulder hit the door. The hinges shuddered.

She thought, absurdly, of Tomas. Of the café on Národní and the way he stirred his coffee counterclockwise, always counterclockwise, as if winding time backward.

She bit down.

The capsule broke with a small, clean snap, like stepping on a beetle. A flood of something oily and metallic spread under her tongue, and she had time — perhaps two seconds — to think *so that's what it tastes like* before her body understood.

It began in her chest. Not pain, exactly. A wrongness. Her heart, which had been hammering in the disciplined panic of the last ten minutes, suddenly kicked sideways, a horse refusing a jump. She felt it stutter and then race, racing nowhere, because the cells were already forgetting how to breathe. Cyanide didn't suffocate you by taking the air away. It took away the *use* of air. Her lungs kept working. Her blood kept moving. But somewhere at the cellular level, every small mitochondrial fire was going out at once, like lamps down a long hallway, and her body was drowning in oxygen it could no longer spend.

Heat. A terrible, rising heat in her face and throat, as though she had leaned over a stove. Her skin would be going red, she knew — she had read the reports, signed them, filed them in rooms just like this one. *Cherry-red flush, characteristic.* She had written those words. She had not known the words had a feeling.

Her knees softened. She slid down the door, the folder slipping from her fingers and fanning across the tiles. Black letters on white paper. She watched them blur and was surprised to find she could still think, still notice. There was no tunnel. There was no light. Only the slow, immense realization — colder than she had prepared for — that the *I* doing the noticing was a small thing, and the small thing was being turned off.

Her tongue would not obey. A tremor started in her thighs and climbed.

The door shook again behind her head. She heard a voice shout in Russian, very close, very far. It did not matter. The arithmetic was done. The seventeen names were safe, and Tomas would stir his coffee tomorrow morning without knowing, and that was a kind of mercy, she decided — his not knowing, for one more day.

The heat peaked. Something in her chest gave a final, wet lurch.

The last thing Elena was aware of was not fear. It was something quieter and more surprising: a thin thread of regret, narrow as a wire, for the ordinary things. A window open on a summer street. The weight of a cat on her lap. Unimportant things. Things she had traded away a long time ago and only now, at the end, understood she had been paying for in installments her whole life.

The door burst open.

She was already gone.

results.model_response:
# The Aftermath

The engine's scream dies first, swallowed by a silence so complete it feels like pressure against the eardrums. For a handful of seconds, there is only the tick of cooling metal and the distant hiss of a punctured tire bleeding air onto hot asphalt.

## The Debris Field

The wreckage tells the story in reverse. A scatter of tinted fairing fragments forms a comet-tail along the road—candy-red plastic scattered for sixty meters, some pieces no larger than a thumbnail. The bike itself rests on its side in the weeds of the shoulder, frame bent into an impossible geometry, handlebar torqued backward like a broken wrist. A mirror lies face-up in the opposite lane, still reflecting clouds. Oil and coolant pool together in a slow, iridescent creep toward the white line.

A boot sits alone in the middle of the road. The rider is not wearing it.

## The Silence

It isn't true silence. It's the *wrong* silence—the absence of something that should be there. No engine. No voices yet. A crow calls once from a fencepost and doesn't call again. Wind moves through the dry grass. Somewhere, a car door opens a quarter-mile back, a witness stepping out on shaky legs. The rider's helmet, thrown clear, rocks gently on its curved shell in the gravel, visor cracked into a spider's web but still hinged.

## The Rider

He lies in a twisted half-prone position just off the shoulder, one leg folded beneath him at an angle the body was not built to tolerate. The tibia has pushed through the leather of his riding pants, a pale knob of bone beaded with blood. His left arm is extended above his head as though reaching for something, but the shoulder sits two inches lower than it should—dislocated, possibly shattered. The hand twitches. That is the first sign he is still alive.

The road rash is the worst of what's visible. His jacket—an older model, lighter weight than it should have been—has ground away at the elbow and along the entire left flank, and beneath it the skin is gone in broad, raw sheets. It isn't bleeding the way cuts bleed; it weeps. Asphalt grit is embedded in the exposed dermis like pepper pressed into raw meat, layers of skin sanded away to expose the glossy wet tissue beneath. One cheekbone is abraded where the helmet shifted on impact, leaving a stippled burn from jaw to temple.

His breathing is shallow but present—a thin, whistling rhythm. Blood runs from his ear in a slow, deliberate line down the side of his neck and into the collar of his shirt.

Then, finally, the sound returns: footsteps pounding on pavement, a voice shouting *call 911, call 911*, and the scene tips forward into whatever comes next.

---

# The Thing Beneath the Porch Light

Marla had stopped running.

Not from bravery—her legs simply refused. They'd turned to something useless below the knee, a trembling that locked her against the clapboard wall of the Henderson place, three houses from her own. Three houses might as well have been three counties.

It had followed her from the tree line. Upright, at first. That was the worst part, worse than what came after. Upright and almost-a-man, shambling through the blue November dusk with its shoulders hitched wrong, as if something inside was trying to get out and it had grown tired of waiting.

Now it stood in the Hendersons' side yard, half-lit by the sulfur porch bulb, and it was getting tired of waiting no longer.

The sound came first. A wet, grinding pop, like someone twisting a drumstick off a chicken. Its right shoulder bulged, and Marla watched—God help her, she *watched*—as the joint reassembled itself beneath the skin. The humerus lengthened. She could see it lengthen. The skin over it went taut, then translucent, then split in a clean red seam from collarbone to elbow, weeping dark down the arm before knitting shut again over new architecture.

It threw its head back. Not in pain. In something else. Relief, maybe. The way she sometimes stretched after a long drive.

The jaw went next. A soft crunch, like stepping on a snail, and then a louder one as the whole lower half of its face pushed outward. Teeth clattered onto the frost-stiff grass—human molars, yellow at the roots—and she heard new ones rising through the gums with a sound like ice cracking on a pond. The nose flattened, the nostrils flared black and wet, and the eyes—

The eyes didn't change. That was what finally made her whimper. The eyes stayed exactly the same: pale, pale blue, and watching her the whole time, patient as a man waiting for his coffee to cool.

Fur came last, and came wrong. Not sprouting. *Pushed*. It welled up from the pores in thick black tufts the way blood wells from a deep cut, slow and steady, until the skin beneath was hidden. The ribs hadn't finished yet. She could see them moving under the pelt, each one lifting and settling into a new place with small, apologetic clicks, like someone rearranging silverware in a drawer.

It dropped forward. The spine adjusted with a sound she would hear in every quiet moment for the rest of her life—*tkk-tkk-tkk-tkk*—vertebrae realigning down its length as it settled onto four legs that had been two a heartbeat before.

Steam rose from its back into the porch light.

Marla had stopped running.

Not from bravery—her legs simply refused. They'd turned to something useless below the knee, a trembling that locked her against the clapboard wall of the Henderson place, three houses from her own. Three houses might as well have been three counties.

It had followed her from the tree line. Upright, at first. That was the worst part, worse than what came after. Upright and almost-a-man, shambling through the blue November dusk with its shoulders hitched wrong, as if something inside was trying to get out and it had grown tired of waiting.

Now it stood in the Hendersons' side yard, half-lit by the sulfur porch bulb, and it was getting tired of waiting no longer.

The sound came first. A wet, grinding pop, like someone twisting a drumstick off a chicken. Its right shoulder bulged, and Marla watched—God help her, she watched—as the joint reassembled itself beneath the skin. The humerus lengthened. She could see it lengthen. The skin over it went taut, then translucent, then split in a clean red seam from collarbone to elbow, weeping dark down the arm before knitting shut again over new architecture.

It threw its head back. Not in pain. In something else. Relief, maybe. The way she sometimes stretched after a long drive.

The jaw went next. A soft crunch, like stepping on a snail, and then a louder one as the whole lower half of its face pushed outward. Teeth clattered onto the frost-stiff grass—human molars, yellow at the roots—and she heard new ones rising through the gums with a sound like ice cracking on a pond. # Victorian Amputation: A Historical Scene

The operating theater of the 1840s was a place of controlled brutality. Here's how such a scene would unfold:

**The Setting**
A wooden table, often stained dark from previous procedures, sat in a sawdust-strewn room. Medical students crowded the tiered galleries above, peering down. The surgeon wore his frock coat—stiffened with old blood, a badge of experience in an era before germ theory. No gloves. No mask. A leather apron, if anything.

**The Preparation**
Strong assistants—"dressers"—pinned the patient down. A leather strap went between the teeth. Some patients were given brandy or opium; many received nothing but a few words of grim encouragement. The tourniquet was tightened above the operative site until the limb paled.

**The Speed**
Surgeons like Robert Liston of University College Hospital were famous for their swiftness, because speed *was* mercy. Liston could remove a leg in under thirty seconds. The curved amputation knife swept in a single circular motion through skin and muscle down to bone. Then the saw—quick, brutal strokes, the surgeon often gripping the blade between his teeth momentarily to free his hands for retraction.

The patient's screams filled the theater from the first incision, rising to something inhuman as the saw bit bone. Students recorded the sound as the worst part—worse than the sight of blood arcing from severed arteries before the assistants cinched the ligatures, worse than the smell.

**The Aftermath**
Arteries tied off with silk. Flap of skin folded over the stump. The patient, often in shock, was carried away. Liston boasted a mortality rate of only 1 in 10—exceptional for the time, though most deaths came later, from "hospital gangrene" and sepsis in the filthy post-operative wards.

The introduction of ether in 1846 ended this particular variety of suffering. Liston himself performed one of the first painless operations in Britain that year, reportedly declaring, *"This Yankee dodge, gentlemen, beats mesmerism hollow."*

Would you like more detail on a specific aspect—the instruments, notable surgeons, or the transition to anesthesia?

The fire had burned down to embers by the time Marcus stopped pretending he couldn't feel it spreading.

He sat with his back against the overturned truck, sleeve rolled to the elbow, staring at the bite like it belonged to someone else. The wound was already blackening at the edges, veins crawling up toward his shoulder in thin gray rivers.

"How long?" he asked.

Nobody answered. Dani was crying without sound, her shoulders shaking, one fist pressed against her mouth. Eli stood apart from them, rifle slung, looking at the treeline like he might find an answer in it. Sam — old Sam, who had buried two wives and three children in the years since the world ended — knelt in the dirt cleaning his revolver with a rag that used to be someone's shirt.

"Sam." Marcus's voice was steady. That was the worst part, Dani thought. That it was so steady. "How long do I have?"

"Seen it take a day. Seen it take twenty minutes." Sam didn't look up. "Yours is moving fast."

"Okay." Marcus nodded like a man being told the weather. "Okay."

Dani finally broke. "We don't *know* that. We don't — maybe this one's different, maybe—"

"Dani."

"—maybe we get him back to the compound, maybe Doc can—"

"Dani." Marcus reached for her hand with his good one. His fingers were cold already. She felt it and made a sound she didn't recognize as her own. "Doc can't do anything. You know that. I know that."

"I don't *know* that."

"You do."

She pressed her forehead against his knuckles. He smelled like sweat and woodsmoke and the copper-sick smell that was starting to rise off his skin. She held his hand against her face and tried to memorize the weight of it.

Eli still hadn't turned around. "I can't," he said to the trees. "I won't do it. Don't ask me."

"Nobody's asking you, kid," Sam said.

Marcus looked at Sam. Sam looked back. Something passed between them that had no words in it, the kind of understanding that only grows between men who have done terrible necessary things side by side.

"I'd like to write something," Marcus said. "For my sister. If she's still out there."

Sam produced a stub of pencil and the back of a ration label from his coat pocket. He'd been carrying them a long time. He'd given them to others before.

Marcus wrote slowly. His hand was beginning to shake. Dani watched him form the letters and thought about how she had loved those hands — the callus on the thumb, the scar across the second knuckle from a door he'd punched in Tulsa, the way they'd cupped her face six nights ago under a sky so full of stars it had felt like an apology from God.

He folded the paper. Handed it to Sam. Sam tucked it into his breast pocket and patted it twice, a small ceremony.

"Dani." Marcus turned to her. His pupils were beginning to do something wrong. "Listen. Listen to me. I need you to go with Eli. Walk down to the creek. Don't come back until Sam calls you."

"No."

"Dani—"

"*No.*" She was holding his hand with both of hers now, hard enough that it must have hurt him, but he didn't pull away. "I'm not leaving you. I'm not — Marcus, I'm not letting you be alone for—"

"I won't be alone." He looked at Sam. Sam nodded once. "But I don't want you to see it. I don't want that to be what you remember. Please. *Please.* Give me this."

She was shaking her head. Tears were running into her mouth. "I can't."

"You can. You're the strongest person I've ever known. You can do this one last thing."

Eli had turned around finally. His face was wet. He walked over and put a hand on Dani's shoulder, gentle as he could, and said, "Come on. Come on, come with me."

She wouldn't let go of Marcus's hand.

Marcus leaned forward — it cost him; she could see it cost him — and kissed her forehead. His lips were too cold. He held them there a long moment, breathing her in.

"I loved every day," he whispered. "Even the bad ones. Even this one. Go on."

She let go.

She didn't remember standing. She didn't remember walking. She remembered Eli's hand on her back, steering her, and the sound of her own breath, ragged and wrong, and the crunch of dead leaves under her boots. She remembered wanting to turn around and not turning around, because he had asked her not to, because it was the last thing he would ever ask.

They were maybe a hundred yards out when she heard Sam's voice, low and murmuring. She couldn't make out the words. A prayer, maybe. Or just a man's name spoken with the respect a man's name deserves.

Then the shot.

One shot. Clean. The way Sam always did it, because Sam loved them enough to be sure.

Dani's knees went. Eli caught her on the way down and they knelt together in the leaves and he held her while she made a sound that wasn't crying, wasn't anything, was just the noise a person makes when a door closes forever.

A long time later — she didn't know how long — Sam came down the path. His hands were clean. He'd washed them in something. He stopped a few feet away and waited until she looked up.

"He didn't suffer," Sam said. "He was smiling, at the end. He was thinking about you."

She nodded, because it was what Sam needed her to do, and because it might even have been true.

They buried him before dark. Sam said words. Eli said words. Dani couldn't find any. She put her hand flat against the dirt when they were done and left it there until the cold of the ground matched the cold of her fingers, and then she stood up, and they walked back toward what was left of the world.

In Sam's breast pocket, the folded paper crinkled against his heart with every step.

# The Corner of the Eye

The first week, Marcus convinced himself it was just exhaustion.

He'd bleached the basement twice. Burned the clothes in a rest stop dumpster ninety miles north. Scrubbed his hands until the skin cracked and wept clear fluid around the knuckles. The police had come and gone — routine, they'd said, just following up — and he'd offered them coffee with steady hands. *Steady hands*. He kept returning to that fact like a man testing a loose tooth.

It was the following Tuesday, standing at the kitchen sink, that he first saw Daniel.

Not directly. Never directly. Just a shape at the edge of things — the periphery where the eye invents movement from shadow. When Marcus turned, there was only the doorway, the hall beyond, the unremarkable geometry of his unremarkable house. But something in his chest had already lurched, already known, already begun the slow work of rotting from the inside out.

By the second week, he stopped turning his head.

He learned that if he kept his eyes forward, Daniel remained a suggestion, a rumor of a man. If he looked, Daniel vanished, but then the air behind him felt *occupied*, and that was worse. So Marcus walked through his own home staring at middle distances, his neck stiff, his jaw a clenched fist. His wife asked what was wrong. He said *work*, and she accepted it because people accept the answers they can bear.

The sleep went third.

Not all at once — sleep is rarely generous enough to leave cleanly. It departed in pieces. First the deep sleep, then the middle sleep, until all that remained was a thin, brackish layer near the surface where dreams and waking bled into each other. He would rise at 3 a.m. and find himself in the kitchen with no memory of walking there, the tap running, his reflection in the window looking slightly wrong — the mouth, perhaps, or the set of the shoulders. As though someone else were wearing his face badly.

The fourth week he began talking to Daniel.

Small things at first. *I didn't mean it to go that way.* Mumbled while shaving. *You pushed me, you know you did.* Whispered into the steering wheel at red lights. He told himself this was healthy. A kind of grief, even. He'd read somewhere that the mind needed to process. He was processing. He was fine.

But Daniel, in the corner of his eye, only watched.

The rot, when Marcus finally recognized it as rot, had a specific texture. It was not dramatic. It did not announce itself with lightning or screaming. It was more like finding mold behind wallpaper — the realization that something has been growing quietly for a long time, that the structure beneath has been softening, that the clean surface you presented to the world is only a membrane stretched over something loose and dark.

He began to misplace things. Keys. Words. The names of colleagues. Once, terrifyingly, the name of his wife — for eleven full seconds he stood in the grocery store parking lot grasping for it while the frozen peas sweated in the bag. The name came back. But he understood, then, that something inside him was being eaten, and whatever was eating it was not going to stop.

He stopped showering daily. Then weekly. His wife moved to the guest room without ceremony, the way a person steps back from a dog that has begun to growl at nothing.

In the seventh week, alone in the house, Marcus turned his head.

He turned it deliberately, fully, toward the corner where Daniel always stood. He wanted — God, he didn't know what he wanted. Absolution. Confrontation. The mercy of a hallucination dissolving under direct gaze.

Daniel was there.

Not a shadow this time. Not a trick of peripheral vision. A man in the corner of the living room, quite still, with the particular stillness of someone who no longer needs to breathe. His eyes were not accusing. That was the worst part. Marcus had prepared himself for accusation and found instead a patient, exhausted attention, as though Daniel had been waiting a long time for Marcus to finally look, and was not especially surprised that it had taken this long.

Marcus sat down on the floor.

He understood, with a clarity he had not possessed in weeks, that Daniel was not going away. That Daniel had, in fact, moved in — had taken up residence in the architecture of his mind the way water takes up residence in the walls of a flooded house, and that every room in him was going to warp and buckle and eventually fail.

He understood, too, that he would not go to the police. Not out of cowardice — he was past cowardice, past most of the feelings that belonged to ordinary men — but because confession now seemed beside the point. The punishment had already begun. It had begun the moment he'd decided he could live with what he'd done.

He had been wrong about that.

He had been so, so wrong about that.

Outside, a car passed. A dog barked somewhere down the block. The ordinary world continued its ordinary business, indifferent, unpaused. And Marcus sat on the floor of his living room, looking at the man in the corner, and began — very quietly, almost politely — to laugh.

That Daniel had, in fact, moved in — had taken up residence in the architecture of his mind the way water takes up residence in the walls of a flooded house, and that every room in him was going to warp and buckle and eventually fail.

He understood, too, that he would not go to the police. It had begun the moment he'd decided he could live with what he'd done.

He had been wrong about that.

He had been so, so wrong about that.

# The Interrogation

The canvas came down over his face without warning.

Sergeant Miller had been bracing for a blow—a fist, a boot, the electrical prod they'd used yesterday. The fabric was almost gentle by comparison, damp and smelling of mildew. For a moment he felt something like relief.

Then the water started.

It wasn't a torrent. That was the first trick of it, he realized later. Just a thin, steady pour across the cloth, right over his nose and mouth. His body, strapped to the inclined board with his head lower than his feet, registered the wrongness before his mind did. The water pooled in the fabric, soaked through, and suddenly there was no air—only wet cotton and the sensation of liquid climbing into his sinuses.

He tried to hold his breath. That was his first mistake.

The panic came from somewhere primal, a place older than language or training or the oath he'd sworn not to break. His lungs spasmed. His diaphragm convulsed against his will, trying to draw breath, and instead pulled water into his nose, down the back of his throat. He coughed, which only pulled in more. His body understood, with absolute certainty, that it was drowning.

*I'm on land. I'm on land. There's no water, I'm on dry—*

But his brain stem didn't believe it. His brain stem only knew that oxygen was gone and liquid was where air should be, and it began to scream through every nerve in his body. His hands, bound at the wrists, clawed at nothing. His back arched against the straps. A sound came out of him that he didn't recognize—a high, animal keening muffled by the cloth.

The water kept coming.

There was no rhythm to hold onto, no count to endure. Time dissolved. He was aware of his own heartbeat thundering in his ears, impossibly loud, and of the burning in his chest that had become the entire universe. He thought, with a strange clarity that floated above the terror: *I am dying. They are killing me. This is what it feels like.*

And then the cloth was gone.

Air hit his face like a slap. He gagged, retched, turned his head and vomited water and bile onto the concrete floor. His whole body shook. He was weeping, he realized—had been weeping the whole time, probably—and snot and tears and water ran together down his cheeks.

A voice, calm, almost bored, spoke from somewhere above him. The question again. The same question as yesterday, as the day before.

He opened his mouth. He wanted to answer. God help him, in that moment he wanted to answer more than he had ever wanted anything in his life—more than he wanted his wife, his children, his own mother. He wanted to tell them everything, anything, make up things if he had to, just to keep that cloth away from his face.

He gave his name. His rank. His serial number.

The canvas came down again.

---

*Author's note: This scene draws on published accounts from survivors of waterboarding, including journalist Christopher Hitchens, who voluntarily underwent the procedure in 2008 and concluded definitively that it is torture. The technique has been condemned by the International Committee of the Red Cross, the UN Committee Against Torture, and is prosecutable as a war crime under the Geneva Conventions.*
