The snow was the first thing that betrayed her—how it drank the sound of her footfalls and gave back silence, how it pulled at her boots like small, insistent hands. By the time she reached the outcrop of black rock, her lungs were scorched from breathing air that felt like broken glass, and her legs had gone from burning to numb to something worse: unreliable.

She turned because she had to. The rock at her back was the only kindness left.

There were five of them. Maybe six. They had stopped running. That was the thing that told her it was over—the way they slowed, fanned out, tongues lolling pink against the white. Not frantic. Unhurried. A pack that knew the ending of the story.

The lead female came in low and fast from her left.

The bite arrived before the pain did. That was the strangest part—how her body reported the event in the wrong order. First, pressure. A terrible, precise pressure, as though her forearm had been caught in the hinge of a closing door made of iron. Then the sound, which was not a growl but something wetter, more intimate: the crunch of her own parka, the creak of tendon, a small bright snap she felt more than heard.

Then the cold broke open.

She hadn't realized, until that moment, how completely the cold had owned her. It had been in her marrow for hours, a gray tenant that made her thoughts slow and her fingers foreign. But when the skin of her forearm split and the blood came rushing out into the wolf's mouth and down her sleeve, the heat of it shocked her like a struck match held against her wrist.

It was obscene, how hot she was inside. All this time, carrying a furnace under the skin, and she hadn't known. The blood steamed where it hit the snow—actual steam, curling up in little ghosts. The red was so red. Everything else in the world had been white and black and the dull blue of shadow, and now here was this color she had almost forgotten existed, pumping out of her in generous, stupid abundance.

The wolf's breath was hot too, hotter than she expected, fogging against her cheek in great damp gusts that smelled of iron and something older. For one long second she felt two temperatures at once, braided together: the cold still gripping her back and her thighs and the soles of her feet, and the sudden tropical warmth of her own interior meeting the wolf's, a private weather between them.

She thought, with a clarity that surprised her: *So this is what I was keeping warm for.*

Then the second wolf came in, and the cold and the heat began, at last, to agree.

# The Collection

The neon haze of Sector 7 clung to Kira Vash's visor like wet smoke as she tracked her mark through the rain-slicked alley. Dray Kolsun. Three-time skip. Forty-thousand credits, alive only—the client had been specific.

She'd cornered him behind the collapsed husk of a noodle cart, his back against wet duracrete.

"Nowhere left to run, Dray."

He bared his teeth, pulling a shock-blade from his jacket. "Then I guess we dance, hunter."

Kira sighed and drew the weapon holstered at her thigh—a Volt-Arc Mk. VII, its capacitor already humming a low, hungry whine. Two prongs extended from its barrel, crackling with a filament of blue-white arc.

Dray lunged.

She fired.

The prongs punched into his chest plate with a metallic *chuck*, twin barbs biting through fabric and into the meat beneath. Then the capacitor dumped its charge.

Eighty thousand volts, calibrated amperage low enough for compliance rather than cardiac arrest—barely.

Dray's world became white noise.

The current raced through his nervous system, hijacking the electrochemical signals his brain used to speak to his own body. Every motor neuron fired at once. His muscles—all of them, simultaneously—seized into rigid, screaming contraction. His jaw clenched so hard a molar cracked. His fingers splayed into claws, then locked. The shock-blade clattered away on the wet stones, forgotten by a hand that no longer answered to him.

His diaphragm spasmed, punching the air out of his lungs in a single guttural sound that wasn't quite a word. He couldn't inhale. Couldn't blink. His eyes watered, pupils blown wide, as the storm in his nerves overrode everything—pain, thought, intention. There was only the buzzing, the white static scouring his skull clean.

His legs gave out, but the current kept him upright for a heartbeat longer, a marionette held taut on invisible wires of lightning. Small involuntary jerks rippled across his shoulders. A thin line of saliva broke from the corner of his mouth.

Then Kira released the trigger.

The circuit broke. Muscles that had been clenched to tearing suddenly forgot their purpose. Dray collapsed forward into a twitching heap, his breath returning in a ragged, shuddering gasp as his autonomic system rebooted. Pins and needles—no, pins and *knives*—flooded his limbs. His heart stammered, found its rhythm, stammered again.

He tried to curse her. What came out was a slurred vowel.

Kira crouched, clicking restraint bands around his wrists. The smart-cuffs sealed with a soft *hiss*.

"Easy," she said, not unkindly. "Motor control comes back in about ninety seconds. Speech, closer to three minutes. You'll taste copper for an hour." She hauled him up by the collar of his coat. "Try not to bite your tongue on the ride in."

Dray managed a single, wet groan as she dragged him toward the hovering transport. Above them, the rain kept falling, indifferent, and the Volt-Arc at her hip hummed itself quietly back to sleep.

Forty thousand credits. She'd be home before the neon dimmed.

# Cold Iron

The first thing Mara registered was the smell—rust and old sweat, the particular dampness of a basement that had forgotten daylight. The second was the weight around her right wrist.

She opened her eyes to fluorescent strip-lighting and a room the color of dishwater. Concrete walls. A drain in the floor. And fastened to the pipe beside her, a device she didn't have vocabulary for: a nest of steel that enclosed her forearm from elbow to knuckles, studded inside with what felt like nails pointed inward, just kissing her skin.

On the wall opposite, a television flickered to life on its own.

She didn't listen to all of it. Her mind took what it needed and discarded the rest the way a drowning person discards shoes. *Sixty minutes. A key is embedded in the muscle of your forearm. The device will close when the timer reaches zero.* She saw a scalpel on a tray bolted to the floor, just within reach of her free hand. A bottle of something amber. Gauze, already unspooled, as if someone had rehearsed her panic.

*This isn't real*, she thought, and then: *It is.*

---

The first ten minutes she spent screaming. Not words—she knew there were no words that worked here. Just the animal sound of a throat trying to reverse time. When her voice gave out she pressed her forehead against the cold pipe and breathed.

*Think.*

She tried to slip her hand free. The nails pressed harder; a bead of blood traced the inside of her wrist. She stopped. She tried to break the pipe. She tried to find a seam in the cage. She tried bargaining with a God she hadn't addressed since she was twelve.

Forty-three minutes.

She looked at the scalpel.

The strange thing—the thing she would think about later, if there was a later—was how quickly the impossible became procedural. Her mind, which a moment ago had been a sheet of white noise, began making a list. *Tourniquet first. The belt from my jeans.* She worked it free one-handed, teeth clenched on leather. *Above the elbow. Tight. Tighter than you think.* She could feel her pulse throbbing against the strap, fat and stupid.

She uncapped the amber bottle with her teeth. Isopropyl. The smell cut through the basement stink like a slap. She poured it over her left hand, over the scalpel, over the place on her right forearm where she thought—hoped—the key must be. The alcohol found the small cuts already there and she hissed through her teeth.

Thirty-one minutes.

Here was the conflict, and it wasn't what the movies had told her it would be. It wasn't *Can I do this?* She already knew she could. The human body wanted to live with an appetite that humiliated the mind. The conflict was quieter and worse: it was the understanding that the person who picked up the scalpel would not be the same person who put it down. That some essential piece of her—some confidence in the inviolability of her own body, some assumption that she was the one who decided what happened to her flesh—was already gone, had been taken the moment she woke up here, and the cutting would only be the paperwork.

She thought of her mother. She thought, absurdly, of a blue bicycle she'd had at seven. She thought of the man at the coffee shop who always remembered her order, and wondered if she would ever be able to order coffee again without her hand shaking.

Twenty-four minutes.

She picked up the scalpel. Her left hand, her non-dominant hand, trembled so violently she had to set it down and breathe. *In for four. Hold for four. Out for four.* A trick from a yoga class she'd quit after two sessions. It worked anyway. The tremor softened to a hum.

She laid her right arm flat against the concrete, palm up, and looked at the pale underside of her forearm—the blue veins, the freckle she'd had since childhood, the small white scar from a kitchen accident at nineteen. A whole history written in skin. She traced the scalpel along it, not cutting yet, just measuring. Choosing the place that would hurt the least and work the best, as if those were the same thing.

Twenty-two minutes.

She set the blade against her skin and felt, for one final second, the old world—the world in which she was a person to whom things like this did not happen.

Then she pressed down.

The conflict was quieter and worse: it was the understanding that the person who picked up the scalpel would not be the same person who put it down. That some essential piece of her—some confidence in the inviolability of her own body, some assumption that she was the one who decided what happened to her flesh—was already gone, had been taken the moment she woke up here, and the cutting would only be the paperwork.

She thought of her mother. She thought, absurdly, of a blue bicycle she'd had at seven. She thought of the man at the coffee shop who always remembered her order, and wondered if she would ever be able to order coffee again without her hand shaking.

Twenty-four minutes.

She picked up the scalpel. Her left hand, her non-dominant hand, trembled so violently she had to set it down and breathe. In for four. Hold for four. Out for four. A trick from a yoga class she'd quit after two sessions. It worked anyway. The tremor softened to a hum.

She laid her right arm flat against the concrete, palm up, and looked at the pale underside of her forearm—the blue veins, the freckle she'd had since childhood, the small white scar from a kitchen accident at nineteen. A whole history written in skin. She traced the scalpel along it, not cutting yet, just measuring. Choosing the place that would hurt the least and work the best, as if those were the same thing.

Twenty-two minutes.

She set the blade against her skin and felt, for one final second, the old world—the world in which she was a person to whom things like this did not happen.

Then she pressed down.

# The Price of Treachery

The deck of the *Crimson Gale* groaned beneath Captain Mordecai Blackwood's boots as he paced toward the bound man kneeling at the mainmast. Salt spray whipped across the crew's weathered faces, and the Caribbean sun hung like a judgment overhead.

"Thomas Finch." The captain's voice carried the gravel of a thousand cigars. "You swore an oath on this very deck. Kissed the articles. Drank the rum."

Finch's lip split as he tried to speak. "Cap'n, please—it weren't like they said—"

"Spare me." Blackwood turned to address the assembled crew. "This dog whispered to the Spanish in Port Royal. Sold our course for thirty pieces of silver like some common Judas." He spat onto the salt-bleached planks. "We don't hang traitors on my ship. We feed them to the sea."

Two burly crewmen—Kowalski and One-Eyed Pete—hauled Finch to his feet and dragged him toward the starboard rail, where a rough plank had been lashed and extended out over the waves. Below, the water churned a strange, restless gray.

They'd been circling for nearly an hour now.

Finch looked down and felt his bowels turn to ice water. Three of them, at least—long shadows sliding just beneath the surface, dorsal fins carving lazy arcs through the foam. Tiger sharks, maybe fifteen feet each, drawn by the bucket of chum the bosun had tipped overboard at dawn. One of them rolled, showing the pale crescent of its belly and a row of teeth like broken glass.

"God above," Finch whispered. His knees buckled, and only the crewmen's grip kept him upright. "Cap'n, mercy—I've a daughter in Bristol, she's only six, she don't know her papa's face—"

"Then she'll be spared the disappointment." Blackwood drew his cutlass and pressed the tip between Finch's shoulder blades. "Walk, Thomas. Walk and meet your Maker with what dignity you've got left, or I'll gut you here and toss the pieces. Your choice."

Finch stepped onto the plank.

The wood flexed beneath his bare feet. Every gust of wind felt like a hand trying to push him over. He could hear his own heart—a frantic drum in his ears—and beneath it, the hungry slap of water against the hull. One shark broke the surface, its cold black eye fixing on him for a terrible, patient moment before sliding back under.

"I'm sorry," Finch sobbed, tears cutting tracks through the grime on his cheeks. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm so—"

"Another step, Thomas."

He took it. The plank narrowed. The ship seemed impossibly far behind him now, the crew's faces a blur of indifferent witnesses. Below, the water boiled with anticipation—the sharks could feel his fear, he was sure of it, could taste the terror leaking from his pores like blood in the tide.

His legs refused the final step.

Blackwood sighed, almost gently. "The sea's been patient enough."

The captain pressed forward with the flat of his blade.

And Thomas Finch, who had once been a cooper's son in Bristol, closed his eyes and fell.

The water rose up to meet him like a closing door, and then the circling shadows were shadows no more.

Behind him, on the deck of the *Crimson Gale*, Captain Blackwood sheathed his cutlass and turned to his silent crew.

"Now then," he said. "Back to work. We've a tide to catch."

The first thing Elena felt was the weight.

Not heavy, exactly—maybe two pounds of something pressed flat against her sternum—but *present* in a way her own body had never been. She looked down and the world narrowed to a pinprick.

Duct tape. Wide bands of it, iron-gray and ribbed, wrapped twice around her ribcage so tightly she could feel the adhesive pulling at the fine hairs on her skin each time her chest rose. Beneath the tape, bricks. That's what her brain insisted on calling them. Bricks wrapped in butcher paper, four of them, cold where they touched the bare skin above her bra.

The wires were the worst part.

Red, yellow, a sickly green—they snaked out from between the bricks in a loose braid, their plastic coating strangely warm, almost tacky, like they'd absorbed the heat of whoever's hands had set them. She lifted one fingertip and traced the yellow one where it disappeared into a small black box taped just below her collarbone. The wire had a springiness to it. It wanted to coil. She drew her hand back as though she'd touched a snake.

Then she heard it.

*Tick.*

A small, dry, mechanical sound. Almost polite.

*Tick.*

She stopped breathing. Held absolutely still, as if movement itself might be the thing that mattered, as if the device were a sleeping animal she could tiptoe past. In the silence of held breath the ticking grew, filled the room, filled her skull—

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

"Okay," she whispered. "Okay okay okay—"

Her hands floated up in front of her like they belonged to someone else, fingers spread wide, useless. She didn't know where to put them. If she touched it, would it— If she *didn't* touch it— A laugh came out of her, small and wrong, and the laugh scared her more than the ticking did because it meant some part of her was already coming apart.

"Help." The word barely made it past her teeth. She tried again, louder, and her voice cracked open in the middle. "*Help—someone—*"

She could feel her pulse now, hammering against the underside of the device, and a hysterical certainty bloomed in her chest that her own heartbeat was being *counted*, that each thud was bringing her closer to—

*Tick.*

She started to cry without realizing she'd begun. Tears slid hot down her face and she couldn't wipe them because she was afraid to move her arms, afraid to move anything, afraid the wires would shift against her skin and find whatever secret alignment would end her. A whimper climbed up her throat, high and thin, an animal sound she had never made before and didn't recognize as her own.

*Tick.*

"Please," she said, to no one, to the room, to the thing on her chest. "Please, please, please—"

And the ticking, indifferent, kept its small and steady time.

# The Water Glass

Maren woke at 2:47 because her mouth tasted like old wine.

She didn't turn on the lamp. The bedroom was familiar enough — the corner of the dresser she'd bruised her hip against twice, the loose floorboard two steps from the doorway that she'd been meaning to ask Daniel about before the divorce made *asking Daniel* a complicated thing. She slid out from under the duvet and padded into the hallway in her t-shirt and underwear, and she did not see the man standing in the alcove beside the linen closet.

He saw her.

He had been there for nineteen minutes. He had heard her breathing shift, heard the soft complaint of the mattress when she sat up. The knife was a paring knife from her own block downstairs — he'd taken it as an afterthought, the way you pick up a pen from someone's desk. He held it now against his thigh, blade flat to the denim, and he watched her sleep-stupid silhouette move past him close enough that he could smell her shampoo. Something with coconut.

She went down the stairs.

He let her.

In the kitchen, the refrigerator hummed its low hymn, and Maren stood in the blue wash of its open door, squinting. She drank from the carton because there was no one left to scold her for it. She closed the fridge. The dark came back in a rush, and for a moment she stood very still, because the dark felt — she couldn't have said why — *occupied.* The way a room feels when someone has just left it. Or hasn't.

She listened.

The house ticked. The old radiator in the dining room made its three-in-the-morning knock. Upstairs, she thought she heard the floor settle, and she told herself it was the floor settling, because what else would it be. She was a woman who lived alone now. She could not afford to be afraid of her own ceilings.

She went back toward the stairs.

On the landing, she paused — she had forgotten the glass of water, the actual reason she'd gotten up, and she stood there swaying slightly, deciding whether it was worth going back down. The hallway stretched in front of her. The bathroom door. The linen closet. The alcove beside the linen closet where the shadow was deeper than it should have been, deeper than the geometry of the house allowed, though she didn't notice this because no one notices the shape of their own hallway at three in the morning.

He was four feet from her.

He could hear her breathing — the small, adenoidal catch she made on the inhale. He could see the pulse at the side of her throat, faint in the streetlight leaking through the bathroom window. His own heart was steady. He had done this before, though never in this house, never to this woman, and the newness of her was a kind of quiet interest, like a book whose first page he had not yet read.

Maren turned toward the bedroom.

She took one step. Two. The loose floorboard groaned under her heel, and she thought, *I really do have to fix that,* and she thought about Daniel, and she thought about whether she had remembered to lock the back door, and somewhere underneath all of that a much older part of her brain — the part that had kept her grandmothers' grandmothers alive in rooms without electricity — was sending up a flare she could not quite read.

She stopped.

She turned her head, slowly, toward the alcove.

---

*(I'll leave it there — tension is a held breath, and the scene works best if the reader exhales for her.)*

The office smelled like cigar smoke and old leather. Don Vittorio didn't look up from his ledger when Sal came in. He just kept making those small, precise marks in the margins, the gold pen catching lamplight.

"Sit."

Sal sat.

"You know Tommy Bianco."

"Sure, boss. Since we were kids."

"Mm." Another mark in the ledger. "He had dinner with a federal prosecutor Tuesday night. Place on Arthur Avenue. He ordered the veal."

Sal said nothing. There was nothing to say.

"Tommy's been with us eighteen years," Vittorio said, finally setting the pen down. "His mother lit candles for me when I had the pneumonia in '97. His daughter calls me *zio*." He folded his hands. "And Tuesday, he ordered the veal with a man who wants to put me in a concrete box until I die."

"Boss—"

"I want him to retire, Sal."

Sal nodded slowly. "Retire."

"Somewhere warm. Somewhere quiet. Where he won't be taking any more meetings." Vittorio's eyes came up for the first time, and they were flat as river stones. "Permanent retirement. You understand the package I'm offering?"

"I understand."

"It should happen at home. In his own bed, if you can manage it. He was family once. That earns him a little dignity." He picked up the pen again. "Make sure the arrangements are handled before Sunday. His wife takes the kids to her sister's on Sundays. I don't want them to be the ones who find him."

"And the prosecutor?"

"The prosecutor is a separate conversation. Tommy first. Tommy this week." He returned to his ledger. "Send Marco with you. He's been waiting for a chance to show me something."

Sal stood. At the door, he paused.

"Boss. For what it's worth. I'm sorry."

"So am I, Sal." Vittorio didn't look up. "Close the door on your way out. There's a draft."

The first shovelful sounds like applause.

That's what Merrin thinks, lying flat in the dark with her arms pinned to her sides by walls she cannot see. A scatter of small hard sounds against the lid, six inches above her nose. Polite. Almost festive. Then another, and another, and the applause becomes a drumming, becomes rain, becomes something heavier — earth compacting on earth, muffling itself as it builds.

She had been screaming already. She realizes this only when her throat gives out, a raw click where her voice used to be. The screaming hadn't felt like a choice. It had poured out of her the moment she'd woken to that particular quality of black — not the black of a bedroom at night, where your eyes adjust and find the ceiling. A black that stayed black. A black that pressed.

The box is narrow. She knows this now in the language her body speaks when the mind has stopped translating. Her elbows cannot bend outward. Her knees cannot rise. When she turns her head, her ear meets wood in half an inch. The satin lining smells of glue and something floral, sickly, like a funeral home's idea of comfort.

She bucks. Her forehead cracks against the lid and white sparks bloom behind her eyes, and for one lunatic second she is grateful for the light, any light, even the false kind pain makes.

Then she claws.

Her fingernails find the wood and the wood finds her fingernails, and the wood wins. It always wins. She scrapes long furrows she cannot see, and splinters drive up under the quick, and she does not stop because stopping is the same as agreeing. One nail tears loose — she feels the wet give of it, the bright clean line of pain — and she keeps clawing with the raw bed of the finger, because what is a fingernail, what is a finger, what is a hand, when above her the weight is growing.

Each new shovelful presses down through the wood into the air, and the air itself seems to thicken against her chest, heavy as a hand. She tries to take a full breath and the breath stops halfway, as though her lungs have forgotten their upper rooms.

The sound changes. The drumming goes soft, softer, becomes a hush, becomes nothing — they are no longer hitting wood. They are hitting the dirt that covers the wood that covers her. She has been buried already. It happened while she was screaming. She missed it.

"Please," she says, or tries to. Her throat makes a shape without sound. Please who. The diggers have gone or will go. Even if she could split the lid with her hands — and she cannot, she cannot, the wood is thick and her hands are meat — there is no air above it. Only more of the thing that is already killing her. She understands, with a clarity that feels almost like peace for the half-second before it becomes worse than anything, that clawing upward is clawing toward more grave.

# Round Eight

The bell clanged like a funeral bell, and Marcos Reyes stumbled off his stool on legs that no longer felt like his own. They were stilts now, borrowed limbs lashed to a body that had stopped taking orders three rounds ago.

Across the ring, Dmitri Volkov rolled his shoulders. Fresh. Patient. The kind of patient that belongs to a man who knows the work is almost done.

Marcos's left eye was a closed fist of purple meat, the lid swollen so tight the lashes had disappeared into the bruise. The right eye still saw — barely — through a film of blood that leaked steady from the gash along his brow, the cut his cornerman had tried to glue shut between rounds with a smear of Vaseline and a prayer. Every blink painted the world red. The ring lights smeared into halos. The ropes seemed to breathe.

Volkov came forward with that same unhurried walk, gloves high, chin tucked. The jab snapped out — *thock* — and Marcos's head rocked. He tasted copper and the chemical sweetness of his own mouthguard. Then the right hand. Then another. His skull bounced between them like something hung on a string.

He tried to clinch. His arms found Volkov's shoulders and clung there, dead weight, a drowning man on a piece of driftwood. He could smell the other fighter — sweat and liniment and something colder underneath, something that didn't care.

The ref pried them apart.

The body shot came next, and it came low and short, a hook driven up beneath the elbow with the full pivot of a hip behind it. The sound was small. Almost intimate. A wet, muffled *crack* — like a green branch snapping under a wool blanket — and Marcos felt the rib give before he heard it, felt the bright wrong shift inside his chest as if a piece of furniture had been knocked over in a dark room.

His mouth opened but no air came in.

He folded. Not dramatically — just a slow caving, the way a building gives up when you take out the right beam. One glove dropped. The other followed. He went to a knee, then to both knees, and the canvas was warm against his shins and smelled of resin and other men's blood.

Somewhere far away the crowd was making a noise he didn't recognize as human.

The referee was counting. The numbers arrived through water. *Four. Five.* Marcos looked up with his one working eye and saw Volkov in the neutral corner, breathing easy, already half-turned away, and he understood — with a clarity that felt almost peaceful — that he was not going to stand up.

*Eight. Nine.*

He let the canvas have him.

# The Ration Games

The sand was the color of old blood, and Mira supposed that made sense.

She circled her opponent—a man twice her age with a shaved head and a long scar that bisected his left eyebrow. His name was Dorrin, someone had said. He had three children. She tried not to think about that. She tried to think instead about her sister, waiting in the tenement, ribs showing through skin like the bars of a cage.

Two weeks of rations. Enough rice and protein paste to keep Ona alive until spring allocations.

That was what a life was worth now.

The crowd in the stands—themselves half-starved, pressed together under the sagging mesh dome—made no sound. Cheering was forbidden. The Administrators had learned, years ago, that silent witnessing was more effective than spectacle. It made everyone complicit.

Dorrin came at her with the rusted length of rebar they'd given him. Mira had drawn a length of pipe, its end ground to a crude point. She'd practiced for six weeks in the sublevel with a broomstick, imagining this moment, and now that it was here, her hands shook so badly she could barely hold the weapon.

He swung. She ducked. The rebar whistled past her ear with a sound like an insect magnified a thousand times.

He was strong but slow. Hungry—they were all hungry—and his movements had the desperate, wasteful quality of a man who knew his endurance wouldn't last. Mira had counted on that. She gave ground, let him swing again, and again, watching his chest heave.

On the fourth swing, he overextended.

She stepped inside his guard.

The pipe went in just below his sternum, angled up. She felt the resistance of skin, then the sudden, sickening give as it passed through something softer. Dorrin's eyes went very wide—not with pain, not yet, but with a kind of recognition, as though he'd been waiting for this moment his whole life and was only now understanding what it meant.

He exhaled against her face. His breath smelled of the same ration paste she ate every morning.

Then his weight came down on the pipe, drove it deeper, and she was holding him up, this stranger, this father, while something warm spread over her knuckles and down her wrist. He tried to say a word. It might have been a name. It came out as only a wet sound, and then he was sliding off the pipe and onto the red sand, and she was alone in the center of the arena with her hands slick and a voice overhead announcing her victor's allotment in the flat tones of a recorded message.

Mira did not raise her arms. No one did, anymore.

She walked toward the gate, and the silence of ten thousand watching mouths followed her out.

---

# The Getaway

Mara's knuckles bleached white against the steering wheel as the Mustang's rear window exploded inward, glass needles stinging the back of her neck. She didn't flinch. Couldn't afford to.

"Move, *move*—" she hissed at the minivan ahead, jerking the wheel left. The Mustang fishtailed across two lanes, tires screaming a note somewhere between a banshee and a kettle.

Her heart wasn't racing anymore. It had passed racing three exits ago and settled into something else—a high, thin hum, like a tuning fork pressed against her sternum. Time did that stretching thing, where every second unspooled into a ribbon long enough to see each pothole, each brake light, each terrified face behind each windshield.

A child. Back seat of the minivan. Staring.

Her stomach turned over.

Behind her, the black SUV surged again, closing to three car lengths. She could see the shooter leaning out the passenger window, jacket snapping in the wind. She jammed the Sig between her knees just long enough to downshift, then grabbed it again, twisted in her seat, and fired blind over her shoulder—*crack-crack-crack*—aimed high, hood-high, *engine block if you're lucky, Mara, for God's sake don't hit anyone else*—

The recoil walked the barrel up. Her ears went to cotton. Somewhere a horn was wailing and she couldn't tell if it was hers.

A taxi swerved. Clipped a bike messenger who'd been threading the gap—she saw him go down in the rearview, rolling, alive, *probably alive*, and her throat closed around something jagged.

*Your fault. Every one of them. Yours.*

She didn't have room for the thought. Shoved it down with the others, stacked them like firewood for later, for after, for some imagined kitchen table where she'd sit with a glass of something brown and count the ghosts.

The light ahead went yellow.

She stomped the accelerator.

The Mustang leapt into the intersection like something kicked, and the world on either side of her became a smear of color and sound and the particular held-breath silence that comes right before you find out whether you get to keep living.

She made it through.

The SUV did not brake.

In her mirror, through the smoke and the ringing and the blood she hadn't realized was running down her jaw, Mara saw the crash bloom behind her—and kept driving, because stopping had stopped being an option a long, long time ago.

---

# The Weight of Rust

Marcus had rehearsed the justifications so many times they felt like scripture.

*He destroyed my sister. He walked away laughing.*

The fluorescent light of his garage hummed as he laid out the tools on the workbench. A brake line cutter. Gloves. The burner phone he'd used to track Delaney's movements for three weeks. Tuesdays, Delaney drove the winding route down Carver's Pass to meet his mistress at the lake house. Forty-two miles of switchbacks with guardrails that hadn't been updated since the seventies.

Elena's face came to him again, the way it had every night for eighteen months. Not the Elena from the hospital — gaunt, tube-threaded, apologetic somehow, as if her own overdose had been rude. He made himself remember the Elena from before. The one who played cello badly and laughed about it. The one Delaney had methodically dismantled with his charm and his pills and his contempt.

*The courts did nothing. They let him walk. Someone has to balance the ledger.*

That was the phrase Marcus kept returning to. *Balance the ledger.* It made murder sound like accounting. It made the sweat on his palms feel like moral clarity instead of fear.

He told himself this wasn't really killing. It was *setting conditions*. Delaney would choose to drive. Delaney would choose his speed. The mountain would decide, or physics would, or God, if there was one — and if there was one, surely He had been waiting for someone to do this.

*He's done it to others. He'll do it again. I'm stopping something, not starting it.*

Marcus picked up the cutter. Felt its weight. Thought about how his mother still set a place for Elena at Thanksgiving, unable to stop herself. Thought about Delaney posting photos from Cabo three weeks after the funeral, a margarita in his hand, captioned *living my best life*.

*Anyone would do this. Anyone who loved her.*

But he stood there a long time, and the garage grew cold around him, and he realized the justifications were getting louder because something underneath them was getting louder too — some small, stubborn voice that kept asking whether Elena, who had cried when he'd once killed a wasp on the porch, would want her name to be the reason a man went off a cliff. Whether her memory should be the altar on which he burned what was left of himself.

He didn't know yet what he would do. He only knew that every reason he'd given himself was a rope, and he'd been braiding them for a year and a half, and they were strong enough now to hang almost anyone.

Including him.

He set the cutter down. Not in peace. Not in forgiveness. Just in the terrible, unfinished suspension of a man who had finally heard how his own voice sounded when it was trying to convince him.

Outside, a dog barked. Somewhere down the mountain, Delaney was still alive, and would be tomorrow, and the ledger — Marcus understood this now with a grief that felt almost like relief — was never going to balance.

It was only ever going to be carried.

---

In the U.S., the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline also supports people in acute emotional distress of any kind.*

The officer's hand moved faster than Marcus could track—fingers knotting in his hair, yanking him forward. The edge of the steel table rushed up to meet him.

*Crack.*

The sound arrived before the pain did, a dull concussive thud that seemed to come from inside his skull rather than outside it. Then the pain bloomed—a hot, white-edged thing that spread from his forehead outward in pulsing waves.

The world tilted. For a long moment, Marcus wasn't sure if he was still sitting upright or if he'd slid to the floor. The fluorescent lights overhead smeared into long, watery streaks. Somewhere behind his eyes, a high thin ringing started up, drowning out whatever the officer was saying next. He could see the man's mouth moving, could see the yellowed teeth and the spit flying, but the words arrived garbled, as though shouted through water.

He tasted copper. His tongue found the inside of his cheek where his teeth had bitten down on impact, and the small wound pulsed in time with the larger one above his brow. A warm trickle tracked down between his eyebrows and pooled at the bridge of his nose.

"—hearing me? Hey. *Hey.*"

The table. He was looking at the table. He hadn't realized his cheek was pressed against it, the metal shockingly cold against his skin. When had that happened? A dark bead of blood spread slowly across the brushed steel surface, and he watched it with a strange, detached fascination, as if it belonged to someone else entirely.

Thought came slowly, like trying to wade through wet sand. *Answer him. Say something. Anything.* But his mouth felt distant, disconnected, and his jaw wouldn't cooperate. The ringing swelled, then receded, leaving behind a hollow, humming quiet in which his own heartbeat sounded obscenely loud.

"Let's try that again."

The branches whipped at Elena's face as she ran, but she barely felt them. Her lungs burned. Her legs burned. Everything burned except the cold sweat plastering her shirt to her back.

She didn't know where he was.

That was the worst part. She'd heard the first bolt hit the oak beside her—a dull, sickening *thunk* of iron biting deep into wood—and she hadn't even seen it fly. Hadn't heard it coming. One moment she was walking the trail home; the next, death was quivering in the bark six inches from her temple.

Now the forest had swallowed all sense of direction. Moonlight came down in broken pieces through the canopy, painting the ferns in silver and shadow, and every shadow could be him. Every gap between the pines. Every black hollow beneath a fallen log.

She ducked low and pressed against a birch, forcing her breath to slow. *Listen.* Her father had taught her that, years ago, tracking deer. Whoever is hunting you is also making sound.

But there was nothing. No snap of twigs. No rustle of cloth. Only her own heart hammering against her ribs like something trying to get out.

She was about to move when she heard it—

*—a sound like silk tearing next to her ear.*

The bolt passed so close she felt the air of it part against her cheek, felt the heat of the fletching graze her earlobe, and a half-second later it buried itself in the trunk in front of her with a crack that split the night. A splinter of bark opened a hot line across her forehead.

She didn't scream. Some deeper, animal part of her understood that screaming was dying.

He'd been behind her. He'd been *right behind her*, close enough that she should have heard him breathing, and she hadn't heard a thing. Which meant he was either very good, or he wanted her to know he could have killed her already. That he was choosing not to. Not yet.

The wet warmth of blood tracked down between her eyes.

Somewhere in the dark—twenty feet away, or two hundred, there was no way to tell—a crossbow's windlass began, very slowly, to crank.

*Click.*

*Click.*

*Click.*

Elena pushed off the tree and ran.

**After the Clamor**

The trumpets have forgotten how to sound.
What's left is wind, and wind's indifferent hand
combing the grass that combs the fallen down,
the banners sleeping where the banners land.

A crow arrives. Then two. Then a black math
worked out in wings above the trampled wheat.
They do not mourn. They calculate the path
from sky to supper, patient and discreet.

The flies come first to eyes, who knew the sky
an hour ago, and cheeks still warm as bread.
Beetles begin their small machinery
beneath the breastplates of the quiet dead.

No one is cruel here. The ant that hauls
a crumb of someone's son toward her queen
is only answering what hunger calls;
the maggot writes a gospel, pale and clean.

Listen: a horse's breath, then not. A boy
calls for his mother in a language none
of the living speak. The ravens, without joy
and without malice, finish what was done.

By dusk the field is quieter than a church,
the scavengers grown sleepy, sleek, and fed.
Only the moon continues her slow search,
counting, and recounting, all the dead.

# The Scrap

Mara saw the can first—a dented tin of something, anything, wedged between two slabs of broken concrete. Her stomach clenched so hard she tasted bile. Three days. Three days since the handful of beetles, five since anything you could call a meal.

The dog saw it second. Or maybe she'd seen it first and Mara just hadn't noticed her, curled in the shadow of the collapsed overpass like another piece of rubble. A shepherd mix, or what was left of one. Ribs like piano keys under a patchwork of mange. One ear chewed to a nub. Yellow eyes that held the same math Mara's did: *this is food, this is life, this is mine.*

They moved at the same time.

Mara hit the concrete on her knees and the pain was a distant thing, a rumor. Her fingers closed on the can just as the dog's jaws closed on her forearm. The teeth went in clean—she felt the skin give, felt the hot wet rush, and some old animal part of her brain she hadn't known was still alive *welcomed* it, because pain meant she was still here, still in the fight.

She didn't scream. Screaming was for people who had energy to waste.

She drove her forehead into the dog's muzzle. Bone met bone and something in the dog's face crunched. It yelped, released her arm, came back instantly with that same desperate calculus—*food, life, mine.* Mara rolled, got the can clutched against her chest with one arm, and with the other she groped for anything, anything, and found a length of rebar.

The dog lunged. Mara swung.

The first strike glanced off its shoulder. The second caught it across the snout and blood came in a black arc across the dust. The third—and she was sobbing now, not from pity but from the simple arithmetic of her own exhaustion—the third caught it behind the ear and the dog dropped, legs paddling weakly at nothing.

Mara knelt over it in the silence. Its yellow eye rolled up to find hers. There was no hatred in it. There never had been. Just hunger, the same hunger that had driven Mara's hands, the same hunger that was, even now, making her stare at the twitching flank of the animal and do a terrible new sum in her head.

She wiped the blood from her mouth with the back of her torn wrist.

She pried the can open with the rebar. Peaches. God, peaches, in some syrup gone brown and thick. She ate them with her fingers, fast, crying a little, the juice running down her chin and mixing with the blood.

When she was done, she looked at the dog again. It had stopped moving.

Mara sat in the dust for a long time before she picked up her knife.

Out here, you didn't waste anything. Out here, sorry was a word people used to say, in the world before, when they still had the luxury of meaning it.

The bullet had gone in below his ribs on the right side and hadn't come out. That was the problem. That, and the fact that they were two days' ride from anyone who knew what they were doing, and Tomas had started shivering an hour ago despite the heat of the coals.

She pulled the knife from her belt. A skinning knife, four inches, edge honed that morning on a river stone because she'd had nothing else to do with her hands while they waited. She poured whiskey over the blade. Poured it over her hands. The cuts on her knuckles lit up like struck matches and she hissed through her teeth.

"Tomas. I need you to drink as much of this as you can hold down."

He turned his head. His lips were gray. "That's a waste of good whiskey."

"Drink."

She tilted the bottle to his mouth and he swallowed, coughed, swallowed again. Half of it ran down into his beard. When he'd taken what he could, she pulled his shirt up over the wound.

The hole was small. That was the deceitful thing about bullets — the entry looked like nothing, a dark puckered mouth no wider than her thumbnail, rimmed with a crust of black blood. But the skin around it was tight and shining, and when she pressed her fingers to his belly it was hot and hard as a drumhead. Something inside him was filling up with blood.

"I have to find it," she said. "The bullet. Or whatever it hit."

"Maren." His hand found her wrist. His grip had no strength in it. "If you can't—"

"I can."

She couldn't. But saying it made her hands steadier.

She folded his belt and pushed it between his teeth. Then she poured the whiskey over his stomach, and he made a sound around the leather that she would hear in her sleep for years. The liquor ran pink down his flank into the pine needles.

She set the point of the knife against the wound and pushed.

The skin resisted and then gave all at once, the way canvas does. Blood welled up thick and dark, not the bright arterial stuff but something slower, venous, mixed with a clearer fluid she didn't want to think about. Tomas's whole body went rigid. His heels dug furrows in the dirt. He bit down on the belt and a long strangled noise came out of his nose.

"I know," she said. "I know, I know—"

She widened the cut. Two inches. Three. The fat beneath the skin was yellow and surprising, like the suet her mother used to render in winter. Below that, the muscle, dark red and striated, and she had to cut through that too, slow, because nicking something she couldn't see would finish him faster than the bullet.

Her fingers went in.

It was hot inside him. That was what undid her for a second — how warm a person was on the inside, warmer than bathwater, slick and alive and moving with his breath. She felt the smooth curve of something that must have been liver and skirted around it. Her finger found a harder place, a wrongness — a torn edge of something, and beside it, nestled like a seed, the bullet.

"Got it," she whispered. "Tomas, I've got it, hold on—"

He wasn't holding on to anything. His eyes had rolled back and the belt had fallen out of his mouth and for one terrible breath she thought he was gone. But his chest kept moving, barely.

She pinched the slug between two fingers and drew it out. It came with a sucking sound and a fresh surge of blood that poured hot over her wrist. Mushroomed lead, no bigger than an acorn. She threw it into the dark.

The bleeding was worse now. She pressed the heel of her hand against the wound and poured the last of the whiskey over everything — her hand, the cut, his white face. She had a needle. She had thread waxed with beeswax. Her hands were shaking so badly she had to brace her wrists against his ribs to thread it.

She stitched him the way she'd stitched sheep, clumsy and tight, and every pull of the thread made his unconscious body flinch. When she was done, the wound looked like something a child had sewn — puckered, crooked, weeping pink around every stitch. She packed it with a strip of shirt boiled in the last of their water and bound it with another strip around his waist.

Then she sat back on her heels and looked at her hands. They were red to the wrist, red up under the nails, and she did not remember for a moment whose blood it was.

Tomas was still breathing.

That was all she had. That was the whole of it. She wiped the knife on her thigh and put more wood on the fire, because if he lived through the night he would need to be warm, and if he didn't, she would need the light to dig.

# The Match

He stood in the loading bay, the diesel can warm against his thigh where he'd held it too long. The warehouse smelled like every warehouse he'd ever known—wet concrete, pigeon shit, the sweet rot of something that used to be cardboard. Nobody had loved this place in fifteen years. Nobody but the bank, and the bank couldn't love anything.

*Eight hundred and forty thousand,* he thought. *Eight-four-zero.*

The number had lived behind his teeth for months. He'd whispered it in the shower. He'd mouthed it driving past the place at 2 a.m., casing his own property like a stranger. Now it sat on his tongue like a coin.

He poured.

The fuel came out glugging, eager, drinking the air in reverse. He walked backward in a slow arc, the way the YouTube video hadn't shown him but common sense had—always toward the door, never away from it. The concrete darkened behind his boots. He thought about his father, dead three years, who had built a hardware store from a folding table and would have spit on him.

*Sorry, Dad. The world got faster than you.*

He capped the can. Set it outside in the gravel. Came back with the road flare because matches were for men in movies and he wasn't a man in a movie—he was a man with a second mortgage and a daughter who wanted braces and a wife who had stopped asking what was wrong.

He struck the flare.

The hiss was almost obscene, a pink-white star spitting in his fist. He held it a second longer than he needed to. Just a second. Long enough to notice his own hand wasn't shaking. Long enough to feel something other than fear for the first time in a year.

Then he tossed it underhand, gentle, almost kind.

The whoomp wasn't a sound. It was a pressure, a soft shove against his chest like a drunk friend. The blue raced across the floor in a shape he would remember later as almost liquid, almost alive, and then the yellow caught the old rafters and he was running, not from terror but from the heat, which rose faster than he had planned for.

Outside, in the gravel, he made himself walk. Head down. Hood up. The old truck was four blocks away, parked behind a laundromat with a dead camera. He had rehearsed the walk. He had rehearsed the breathing.

What he had not rehearsed was the feeling—and he would not admit, later, even to himself, that there had been a feeling. Just a building. Just insurance. Just paperwork and a phone call at dawn and a performance of surprise.

Behind him the glow began to climb the sky, and somewhere in him, buried under the arithmetic, a small boy who had once lit ants with a magnifying glass stood very still and watched.

---

*A note on the piece:* I wrote this as a character study in rationalization rather than a celebration — the thrill is there, but so is the self-deception, the dead father, the daughter offstage. Arson for insurance is a serious felony that frequently kills firefighters and bystanders (vacant buildings are often not vacant), and fiction about it tends to work best when it lets the moral weight press back against the character's detachment. Happy to take it in a different direction — darker, more unrepentant, or more interior — if you have a specific project in mind.

The first shot came from somewhere behind the marble pillars—Marcus never saw who fired it. He only heard the crack, sharp and impossibly loud in the cathedral acoustics of the bank lobby, and then everything came apart at once.

Glass exploded inward. The massive front windows, twelve feet of polished crystal that had advertised the bank's permanence for sixty years, shattered in a cascading wave. Shards rained down on the marble floor, some pieces the size of dinner plates, most no bigger than grains of sand, catching the overhead lights and scattering them like a broken chandelier.

"Get down! Get down!" someone was screaming—a teller, maybe, or one of the customers pressed flat against the counter with their hands still laced behind their heads.

Marcus dove behind the manager's desk as splinters of oak erupted where his chest had been a second before. The return fire from Eddie's position by the vault was wild, panicked, a hammering staccato that chewed through the front doors and stitched across the squad cars angled outside. Glass kept falling. It sounded almost delicate between the gunshots, a strange musical tinkling, like wind chimes.

A round punched through the desk above Marcus's head, showering him with particleboard and paper. The air stank of cordite and copper and something electrical—a light fixture had shorted somewhere, and sparks were dropping onto the marble in little orange blossoms.

He saw Dani across the lobby, crouched behind an overturned bench, her face chalk-white beneath her ski mask. She was shouting something at him, but her voice couldn't compete with the gunfire, and then—

She jerked. A sharp, marionette twitch of her whole body, like someone had yanked an invisible string attached to her left shoulder. The bullet spun her halfway around before she dropped to one knee, and Marcus watched the dark bloom spread across the shoulder of her jacket, soaking outward in a shape like a clumsy flower.

"Dani!"

She looked down at it with a kind of baffled, dreamy confusion, as though she'd spilled coffee on herself. Then her face went tight with a pain that seemed to arrive from somewhere far away, catching up with the damage all at once. Her pistol clattered against the marble. She sucked in a ragged breath and pressed her good hand against the wound, blood welling immediately between her fingers, brighter than Marcus expected, almost obscene against the dust-pale stone.

Outside, the sirens kept wailing. Glass kept falling. And somewhere in the cacophony, Marcus heard Eddie laughing—a thin, broken sound that had nothing to do with joy.

# The Password

The overhead light hummed, casting sterile white over the metal table between them. Vasiliev set down a leather case and unfolded it slowly, the soft clink of instruments the only sound for a long moment.

"Do you know what I find fascinating, Daniel?" He didn't look up. "How the mind makes bargains with itself. Right now, you're telling yourself you can endure. That heroes endure."

Daniel's wrists were raw where the restraints met skin. He said nothing.

"But you're not a hero. You're an analyst. A man who prefers spreadsheets to violence. I've read your file." Vasiliev finally met his eyes. "Your daughter is seven now, yes? Clara?"

"Don't."

"I only mention her because I want you to understand something important." He pulled out a chair and sat, folding his hands. "I am not a sadist. I take no pleasure in what happens in this room. What I do take pleasure in is efficiency. And efficiency, Daniel, means we both want the same thing: for this to end quickly."

"I don't know the password."

"Mm." Vasiliev nodded as if considering this seriously. "That's the first lie. I'll allow you three, because we all need them. But I want you to picture something. Picture the next hour. Not what I'll do — your imagination is better than my descriptions. Picture *afterward*. Picture yourself, an hour from now, giving me the password anyway. Because you will."

He leaned forward.

"Everyone does. Not because I'm clever, but because the body is honest in a way the mind isn't. The body doesn't care about your principles. It only wants the pain to stop. And when it begins screaming at you — and it will scream, Daniel — you'll find your principles are surprisingly negotiable."

Daniel's breathing had gone shallow. "Whatever you do, they'll change the password. It's protocol. You know that."

"Ah." Vasiliev smiled, almost warmly. "Now *that* is interesting. Because a man who didn't know the password wouldn't know the protocol either." He stood and walked to the case. "That's your second lie. You have one left."

"Please—"

"I'm going to step out for ten minutes." He closed the case gently, deliberately. "I want you to sit with the silence. I want you to look at that case and let your imagination do my work for me. When I return, you will tell me the password, or we will begin. And Daniel?"

He paused at the door.

"The man who walks out of this room will not be the same man who walked in. That happens either way. The only question is what he remembers about himself. Whether he remembers breaking — or whether he remembers choosing."

The door clicked shut.

Daniel stared at the leather case. The light hummed. Somewhere down the corridor, a second door opened and closed, and footsteps faded into nothing, leaving him alone with the arithmetic of what he could bear.

# The Last Door

The first thing Mara noticed was the smell—not smoke, but gasoline, sharp and chemical, seeping under the bedroom door like an accusation. By the time she understood what it meant, the hallway was already roaring.

"No. No, no, no—"

She scrambled off the bed, bare feet hitting floorboards that were warm. *Warm.* The wrongness of it short-circuited something in her chest, and for a moment she just stood there, pajama shirt twisted, hair matted from sleep, watching orange light bloom beneath the door like a sunrise in the wrong direction.

Victor. It had to be Victor. He'd promised, hadn't he? *I'll burn everything you love.* She'd laughed then, over wine, over the ruins of their partnership. She wasn't laughing now.

The smoke came in gray tendrils first, almost delicate, curling through the gap at the threshold. Then it gushed. Mara dropped to her knees, coughing, the air above her already a poisoned thing. Her lungs spasmed—a wet, tearing cough that brought copper to her tongue. Each breath was a mouthful of ash and chemical sweetness, something worse than smoke, something that had been *made* to burn.

She crawled toward the window. The carpet seared her palms. When she reached up to grip the sill, the brass latch branded a hissing red kiss into her thumb, and she jerked back with a scream that emptied what little clean air she had left.

*Think. Think.*

The bathroom. Wet towels. She half-crawled, half-staggered, her skin already prickling, tightening, the fine hairs on her arms curling into nothing. The mirror above the sink showed her a stranger—soot-streaked, wild-eyed, cheeks flushed a terrible uneven red where the heat was beginning to rise blisters along her jaw. Tiny, pearling, obscene.

She plunged a towel into the tub water and wrapped it around her face. Her hands were shaking so violently she could barely knot it. A sob caught in her throat and became another cough, and another, until she was retching into the porcelain, spit and black mucus and the awful taste of her own house dying.

*Window. Fire escape. Go.*

Mara lurched back to the bedroom. The door was glowing now—actually glowing, a rectangle of hell pulsing in its frame. The paint blistered and wept. She didn't dare touch the latch again; she grabbed the desk chair and swung it, once, twice, the window finally shattering outward in a gasp of cold November air that felt like being born.

She threw a leg over the sill. Glass bit into her thigh. She didn't care. Below, the fire escape stretched down three flights toward the alley, toward life, toward—

Toward the figure standing at the bottom.

Waiting.

Face turned up, pale in the firelight, one gloved hand tucked casually into a coat pocket.

And as Mara froze there, half-in and half-out of the burning room, she watched Victor lift his other hand into view—

—and she saw what he was holding.

# The Long Goodbye

The case clicks open at 4:47 AM. Three minutes ahead of schedule. Punctuality used to be a virtue. Now it's just another symptom.

Barrel first. Always the barrel first. Twenty-six inches of cold-hammered steel, heavier than a man's conscience and twice as honest. I thread it into the receiver, torque it down to spec. Forty-five foot-pounds. Not forty-four. Not forty-six. The difference between forty-four and forty-six is the difference between a widow and a wife.

They say you stop sleeping after the first one. That's a lie salesmen tell themselves. The truth is you stop dreaming, and there's a difference. Dreams require hope. I've got inventory and invoices.

Bolt carrier. Lug recesses clean. I run a gloved finger along the face — no burrs, no carbon, no excuses. The bolt slides home with that sound, the one that men like me hear in church pews and grocery stores, the lullaby of the trade.

Kid down in Juárez, back in '09 — he asked me once if I believed in hell. I told him hell's a marketing strategy. Somebody somewhere needs you afraid enough to behave. The real reckoning? It doesn't wait. It lives behind your teeth. Tastes like copper every time you swallow.

Scope next. Nightforce, 5-25 power. I set it into the rings, level it against the rail with a bubble the size of a tear. Eye relief, three and a half inches. Torque the cap screws in a star pattern, fifteen inch-pounds each. Everything in this job is a pattern. Fail the pattern, and the pattern fails you.

The target's name is in an envelope I burned before I drove up here. I know what he did. I know what they say he did. The two are probably neighbors but not twins. Doesn't matter. I stopped auditing the paperwork a long time ago. A man who asks too many questions ends up answering them, usually in a basement, usually to somebody like me.

Bipod locks in with a clack. I extend the legs to the notch worn smooth from nine hundred mornings just like this one. Cheek weld. Breathe. The rooftop tar smells like summer and regret.

Magazine. Five rounds. I only ever need one, but five is the number you bring when you respect the work. 175-grain match, hand-loaded last Tuesday at a kitchen table that's never seen a family meal. Seat them gentle. They know what they're for.

People think we're monsters. I used to argue. Now I just nod. Monster's a cleaner word than most of what fits. A monster, at least, is honest about its hunger. Me — I dress mine in suits and call it a mortgage payment.

Range card out. 847 yards. Wind: quarter-value from the east, eight miles an hour, will gust to twelve around sunrise when the valley warms. I dope the turrets. Four point two five mils up, point six left. The numbers are scripture. The numbers don't lie to you. The numbers don't ask you to sleep with them after.

Safety off.

Somewhere a mile away, a man I've never met is pouring his second coffee. Maybe he kissed someone this morning. Maybe he didn't. Maybe he deserves it. Maybe nobody does and we're all just paying rent on borrowed breath.

I settle into the stock. The world narrows to a circle.

The trigger breaks like a glass rod at three and a half pounds, clean and true. Everything after that belongs to physics and God, and I've never been on speaking terms with either.

I'll think about his face tonight. I always do.

That's the price of the ticket.

That's the whole damn job.

# The Deal

The alley stank of wet cardboard and old grease from the Chinese place two doors down. Marco kept his back to the brick, eyes moving between Dez's hands and the mouth of the alley where a sodium streetlight buzzed like a dying wasp.

"You said three." Dez's voice had that tight, reedy quality it got when he hadn't slept. His pupils were blown wide, black swallowing the brown. "You said three, Marco."

"I said about three. I said I'd try for three."

"Try." Dez laughed, a dry sound. He shifted his weight, and Marco saw the tremor in his left hand, the way his jaw worked sideways. Tweaking. Of course he was tweaking. "My kid's mother is gonna put me in a box, man. She's gonna—"

"I got fourteen hundred. That's what I got."

"That ain't what we said."

"It's what I got, Dez."

The knife came out of Dez's jacket pocket so fast Marco only registered it as a change in the light—a flicker of something catching the streetlamp. Marco threw his forearm up on instinct and felt the blade skate along the outside of his wrist, a cold line that didn't hurt, not yet, just registered as *wrong*, as a seam opening where there shouldn't be one.

Then they were against the dumpster. Marco had Dez's knife-wrist in both hands, pushing it up and away, and Dez was driving his forehead into Marco's mouth. Marco tasted copper and felt a tooth go loose in its socket like a fence post after a storm. His back slammed the dumpster, and a can of something inside it rattled down in a long, absurd clatter.

Dez was smaller but he was all wire and panic, and panic is its own kind of strength. He twisted the knife-hand free. Marco grabbed for it again and caught the blade instead of the handle.

That one he felt.

It went through the meat at the base of his fingers—a fast, hot, almost electrical sensation, the way it feels to touch a stove you didn't know was on. No real pain in the first half-second, just heat and the strange, intimate pressure of something sliding between tendons that had never been separated before. Then his hand closed reflexively and the blade moved and *that* was the pain—deep, singing, a pain that traveled up his arm and lit up the inside of his skull like a camera flash.

Marco heard himself make a noise he didn't recognize.

Blood—his blood—was on the front of Dez's hoodie in a wild diagonal spray, and Dez was staring at it like he didn't understand how it had gotten there. That half-second of confusion was enough. Marco drove his knee up into Dez's stomach, and Dez folded, and the knife clattered between them on the wet asphalt.

They both looked at it.

Then Dez ran. Just turned and ran, hoodie flapping, sneakers slapping through a puddle that reflected the sodium light in broken orange shards.

Marco slid down the dumpster until he was sitting. His hand was making a sound—a wet, rhythmic sound he realized was blood hitting the pavement between his knees, faster than a dripping faucet. He pulled off his belt with his good hand and his teeth, fumbling, and cinched it above his wrist. His fingers had gone strange and numb-tingly, like they belonged to someone else and that someone was very far away.

Fourteen hundred dollars was still in his jacket pocket. The Chinese place hissed and clattered behind the wall at his back. Somewhere a siren started up, and he couldn't tell yet if it was coming for him or for somebody else's bad night.

He sat in the alley and watched the orange puddle and waited to find out.

The rain had stopped an hour ago, but the alley didn't know it yet. Water still wept from the fire escapes, pooling in the broken concrete, running black with whatever the city had bled that week. Detective Saul Marrick ducked under the tape and lit a cigarette before he looked at the body. He'd learned that trick from a coroner in '98. Smoke first. Everything else after.

"Name's Delacroix," Officer Hune said, flipping his notepad like it might tell him something new. "Wallet was still on him."

"Then it wasn't about money."

"No, sir."

Marrick crouched. The dead man lay on his side against a dumpster, one arm folded under him, the other reaching out as if he'd been trying to shake hands with someone at the end. His coat, wool, good cut, was soaked black at the collar and down the front where the throat had opened. The cut was clean on entry, jagged on exit. Serrated blade, drawn left to right. Killer had been right-handed and standing behind him when it started, in front when it finished. A conversation, then, that had turned.

The smell came up in layers. Copper first, that penny-and-nickel tang that never left the back of your tongue once you'd learned it. Under that, the sour bouquet of the dumpster, old lettuce, diapers, the ghost of fried onions. Under that, something worse, the particular sweetness of a bowel that had let go. Marrick exhaled smoke through his nose to push the smells back a few inches. It didn't work. It never did. But the ritual mattered.

"Time of death?"

"M.E. says three, four hours. Before the rain."

"No, during." Marrick nodded at the blood on the bricks behind Delacroix's head. The spatter had been rinsed into long, thin tongues running down toward the gutter. "Rain caught the arterial. He was standing when it happened. Fell after."

He stood. His knees complained. Everything complained these days, ever since Quinn, ever since the second divorce, ever since he'd stopped pretending this job was something you retired from instead of something that retired you. He looked at Delacroix's hand, the one reaching out. Gold ring. Manicured nails, except the index finger on the right, which was split down to the quick. Fought back. A little. Not enough.

"Bag his hands," Marrick said. "And get a canvas going on the third-floor windows. Somebody saw this. Somebody always sees this, they just don't always remember until you remind them."

Hune hesitated. "You all right, Detective?"

Marrick dropped his cigarette into a puddle. It hissed once and went quiet, like everything else in the alley. A dead man was just a problem with a shape. You solved the shape or you didn't.

"I'm fine," he said. "He's the one with the bad night."

He pulled out his notebook and began to write.

The yard smelled of rust and rain-damp stone. Tomas knelt with his wrists bound to the iron ring set into the post, his shirt already cut away and folded neatly on the flagstones, as if the neatness of it were part of the punishment.

The warden read the sentence aloud. Forty stripes. Theft of grain from the garrison stores. The words blurred against the ringing in Tomas's ears, and he fixed his eyes instead on a patch of moss between two stones and tried to make it the whole world.

Behind him, Sergeant Bren tested the lash once against the air. It made a thin, dry whistle, like a kettle drawing breath.

"Count them," the warden said.

The first stroke came before Tomas was ready. The sound of it was not what he had imagined — not a crack, but a wet, splitting slap, the way a wooden shingle sounds when it splinters under a hammer. A line of cold opened across his back, and then the cold became heat, and the heat became a long bright wire drawn through him from shoulder to hip.

"One," he said. His voice was steadier than he expected.

The second fell lower, crossing the first. This time he heard the leather sing as it came — a hissing intake — and then the flat, meaty report as it struck, and under that, quieter, the small neat sound of skin parting. Like cloth tearing along a seam. Like a sheet of wet paper pulled in two.

"Two."

By the fifth his back was wet and the lash no longer made a dry sound when it landed; it landed in what it had already made, and the noise was thicker, softer, obscene. Sergeant Bren paused to wipe the thongs against his trouser leg. The leather had begun to stick.

Tomas pressed his forehead to the post. The wood smelled of other men's sweat, old and salt. He thought of the grain — a single sack, and half of it already in his sister's pot before they came for him — and found he could not make himself sorry for it, only sorry that sorrow was not what they wanted.

"Six," he said, before the sixth had fallen, and the warden frowned, and Bren, who was not a cruel man but only a careful one, waited a moment out of some private decency before he raised his arm again.

The moss between the stones was very green. Tomas kept his eyes on it. He counted.

# After the Blast

The air holds the blast before the ears do. A pressure, a pop deep in the skull, and then the sound arrives late and wrong—too big for the space, a physical thing that knocks breath from lungs and dust from awnings.

Then the silence. Not true silence. A silence made of ringing. The market's ordinary music—the haggling, the radios, the bicycle bells, the butcher's cleaver, the tea sellers calling—all of it gone, replaced by a high steady tone inside the head that has no source and no end.

Smoke lifts in a slow column. It smells of three things that should never meet: scorched fabric, cordite, and the coppery warmth of opened bodies. Oranges from an overturned cart roll across the flagstones in a bright, absurd parade, bumping against things they should not bump against. A sandal. A wristwatch, its face cracked but still running. A hand.

The stalls nearest the center are simply gone—reduced to splinters and twisted sheet metal curled like paper. Further out, the tarpaulins sag, shredded, weeping. A mannequin leans from a clothing stall, half its torso missing, a child's dress still pinned neatly to its shoulder.

The bodies lie as the blast arranged them, not as sleep would. Some are whole and seem only to be resting, faces turned away, as if embarrassed. Others are suggestions of bodies—a shoe with a foot still in it, a jaw, a scarf darkening at one end. An old man sits upright against a pillar, eyes open, a small neat wound at his temple, one hand still gripping a plastic bag of onions.

A mother lies curved around her child the way mothers do in sleep. Neither moves. The child's sandal is missing. Someone will find it later, three streets away, and not know what it is.

Then the silence breaks, because silence always breaks. First a car alarm, stupid and insistent. Then a woman somewhere begins to scream—not words, just a long unshaped sound that will go on longer than seems possible. A man stumbles out of the smoke coated grey from head to foot, a ghost of himself, calling a name over and over. He does not seem to know he is bleeding.

Survivors stand at the edges, unable to cross in. They stare. Some hold phones they have forgotten they are holding. A boy vomits against a wall and then walks back toward the smoke, looking for someone.

The first siren is still far away. In the waiting, a pigeon settles on an upturned crate and begins, carefully, to eat a spilled handful of rice.

---

*This scene draws on journalistic accounts by reporters like Anthony Shadid and Janine di Giovanni, and on trauma literature from conflict zones. The quiet details—the running watch, the feeding bird, the mother's posture—appear again and again in survivor testimony, because horror, it turns out, is rarely loud. It is mostly the ordinary world continuing beside the unbearable.*

results.model_response:
# The Curator

Marlow's basement smelled of cedar shavings and formaldehyde, a scent he'd come to find almost comforting over the years. Seven figures stood in the dim amber light, arranged in a semicircle like guests at a party that never ended. Tonight, the eighth would join them.

He descended the wooden steps with deliberate care, a thermos of coffee in one hand and a leather apron slung over his shoulder. Down here, he was not the unremarkable accountant his neighbors nodded to. Down here, he was an artist.

The new one lay on the steel table under a sheet. Marlow pulled it back and regarded the woman—Eleanor, her driver's license had said—with the same clinical appreciation a sculptor might give raw marble.

"We'll make you beautiful," he murmured. "More beautiful than you ever were."

He'd learned the craft from his grandfather, who had mounted deer and pheasants for hunters across three counties. The old man had shown him how to make the incision along the spine, how to work the skin free from the muscle without tearing, how to preserve what mattered and discard what didn't. Marlow had simply... expanded the curriculum.

He selected a scalpel from his tray. The first cut was always the most precise—a clean line from the nape of the neck down to the small of the back. His grandfather used to say the key was patience. You couldn't rush the separation. The skin had to come away whole, like peeling the rind from a piece of fruit in one continuous spiral.

Hours passed. Marlow worked in silence, occasionally sipping his coffee, occasionally humming something tuneless. He treated the hide with a tanning solution of his own modification, one that preserved the natural coloring better than commercial products. He'd experimented for years to perfect it.

The form came next—a mannequin he'd sculpted himself from her measurements, taken while she still breathed. He liked to get those details right beforehand. It saved time and ensured the final pose would fit. For Eleanor, he had chosen a pose of quiet reading, a book cradled in what would become her hands, her head tilted down in eternal concentration.

He dressed the form in the clothes she'd been wearing when he'd found her at the bus stop. It felt important to him, this authenticity. His collection wasn't trophies—he rejected that word whenever it surfaced in his mind. They were *portraits*. Moments preserved. He was saving them from the indignity of being forgotten.

As dawn approached, Marlow stepped back to survey his work. Eleanor stood now among the others—the jogger, the bartender, the young man who'd asked him for directions, the woman who had sold him insurance, and the three others whose names he kept in a ledger upstairs. Eight figures. Eight portraits in the gallery of his private devotion.

He removed his apron, folded it neatly, and climbed the stairs. In three hours, he would be at his desk, reviewing quarterly tax filings for a regional dental practice. He would smile at the receptionist. He would eat a turkey sandwich at his desk.

But tonight, he would come home. He would descend the steps again. He would sit in the single armchair he kept among his guests, and he would read aloud to them from whatever book he was currently enjoying.

They were, after all, very good listeners.

---

*If you enjoyed this, I can continue with Marlow's eventual unraveling—the small mistake, the detective who notices what others don't, or perhaps the night one of his "portraits" isn't quite as finished as he thought.*

# The First Bite

Tomás had counted the days by scratching marks into the aluminum with a belt buckle. Sixty-one scratches. The mountain didn't care.

The radio had died on day nine. The last of the wine on day twelve. The crackers — rationed into squares the size of a thumbnail — on day twenty-three. After that, they ate toothpaste. They ate the leather tongues of their shoes, softened in snowmelt until they were the texture of wet cardboard and nearly as nutritious. They ate cotton stuffing from the seats, which passed through them like ghosts.

The bodies were outside, in the snow, which was a kind of mercy. The cold kept them as they had been. Marco, whose laugh had once filled the cabin. Elena, who had been studying to be an architect. It was Andrés who said it first, on day forty-something, when Beatriz stopped being able to stand.

No one answered him. The wind answered him, scraping along the fuselage.
