# The Offering

The fluorescent light above the table flickered once, then steadied.

Marcus stared down at the porcelain plate. White. Clean. Rimmed in a delicate blue floral pattern, the kind his grandmother had owned. The domestic normalcy of it made what sat on top worse.

A human heart. Or what he hoped was animal—he'd stopped being able to tell the difference between what he hoped and what he feared twenty minutes ago, when the speaker had crackled to life.

*"To save her, you must take her in. Consume what sustains, and she will be sustained."*

Across the room, behind a pane of reinforced glass smeared with condensation, his sister pressed her palm against the barrier. Her mouth moved. He couldn't hear her. The water around her ankles had risen to her shins.

The clock on the wall read 4:47. He had until 5:00.

Marcus picked up the fork. His hand was shaking so badly the tines rattled against the plate like a small, frantic bell.

The heart was cold. He hadn't expected that. Some stupid part of him had expected warmth, as if it might still be alive, still be beating, and that had felt worse somehow than what he was actually looking at: a slick, purple-brown muscle, veined with yellow fat, its severed vessels gaping like tiny screaming mouths. A thin film of blood pooled beneath it, already congealing at the edges into something darker, tackier.

He cut into it.

The knife went through easier than he expected, then caught on something fibrous. A tendon. He had to saw. The sound was wet and soft, and the smell bloomed upward—iron, yes, but also something gamier, something faintly sweet, like meat left too long in a warm car.

His stomach clenched before the piece ever reached his mouth.

*Don't think. Don't think. Don't think.*

He brought the fork up. Chewed air once, practicing. Lowered it. Raised it again. His mouth wouldn't open. His jaw had locked itself shut in some ancient refusal, the body's older wisdom overriding him.

Through the glass, his sister was crying now. Water at her thighs.

He shoved the piece into his mouth.

The texture hit him first—rubbery resistance, then a sudden give, releasing cold liquid across his tongue. Copper. Salt. Something mineral and deep that coated the roof of his mouth in a film he knew wouldn't wash away for days. He bit down and felt gristle slide between his molars, refusing to break.

His throat closed.

His diaphragm kicked up hard, a violent involuntary spasm, and the heart-meat lurched toward the back of his tongue. He clamped a hand over his mouth. His eyes streamed. He could feel the thing sitting there, refusing to be swallowed, while his body tried to expel it in great heaving waves that made his shoulders jerk.

*Chew. Chew. Swallow.*

He forced his teeth down. The gristle snapped with a small, awful pop, and more cold fluid flooded his mouth, and that was when the retch came—real, full-bodied, from somewhere below his ribs. He lurched forward. Bile rose, hot and sour, meeting the cold meat halfway.

He swallowed against it. Both of them. Down.

It went down like a stone wrapped in wet cloth. He felt it every inch of the way.

Marcus gasped, a single ragged sob, and picked up the knife again.

The clock read 4:51.

---

The air in the temple hung thick with incense and something older—iron, perhaps, or the memory of it soaked into the basalt. Torches guttered in brackets along the walls, and their light did not quite reach the ceiling, which arched into a darkness that seemed to breathe.

The priest descended the seven steps to the altar without hurry. His sandals made no sound. He was an old man, or perhaps only a tired one; the paint on his shaven scalp had cracked along the lines of his skull like a map of dry riverbeds. His eyes, when they caught the torchlight, held nothing—not cruelty, not pity, not even the dim satisfaction of a craftsman at his work. They were the eyes of a man reading a ledger.

The offering lay bound upon the stone: a young ram, its flanks heaving, its black eyes rolling. The priest placed one hand flat against its throat, not to comfort it but to measure the pulse beneath the wool, the way a cook tests the heat of an oven. He nodded once, to no one.

The knife was obsidian, older than the temple itself. He lifted it, spoke three words in a language that predated speech as the acolytes understood it, and drew the blade across the animal's throat in a single, practiced motion. Blood came in a dark arterial rush, steaming against the cold stone, running along the carved channels that spiralled toward the basin at the altar's foot. The ram shuddered. The priest watched it go still the way a man watches rain.

He did not flinch when the warm spray reached his wrist. He did not wipe it away. With the same deliberate economy, he opened the body along its belly, parted the ribs, and drew out the liver to examine it in the torchlight, turning it this way and that, checking its lobes for the signs he had been taught to read before he had been taught his own name.

Whatever he saw there, his face did not change. He set the organ upon the brazier. The smoke rose straight up, and he observed this too, and made a small mark in ash upon the altar's edge.

Then he washed his hands in the prepared bowl, dried them on the linen, and turned to go. The acolytes would handle the rest. He had another rite at dawn.

The cobblestones are warmer than I expected.

That's the first stupid thought, and I laugh at it—or try to. What comes out is wet and small, a sound I don't recognize as mine. Somewhere above me the sky is doing that thing it does at dusk, turning the color of a bruise, and I wonder if I'm looking up or if my eyes have just given up on the task of distinguishing.

My hand is pressed to my side. I told it to go there and it went, good dog, and now it won't come back. The blood is hot at first and then not. It's like sitting in a bath as the water cools and you don't notice until you do, and then you can't notice anything else.

*Thump.*

There. That's me. That's still me.

The alley is narrow and I can see a sliver of the street at the end of it, and people moving past, and none of them look down this way. A woman laughs. A cart rattles. The world has the nerve to keep happening.

Marco is gone. I think I heard him run. Or maybe I heard my own boots scraping as I slid down the wall. The knife is still in my hand—I can feel the grip, I think, though my fingers have become a rumor. I won it. That's the joke. I won.

*Thump. Thump.*

Slower now. I'm listening to it like a song on the other side of a wall. Someone's heart, not necessarily mine. It could belong to anyone. It could belong to the building. Old stones have a pulse if you lie still enough against them.

The cold is coming up from my feet, which is backwards. Cold should come from outside, should sink down through the shoulders and the skull like snow. This cold is climbing me from the inside, room by room, turning off the lights. My knees went a while ago. My belly is a dark lake with no bottom.

I try to think of her face and I can, almost. The shape of it. The way she tucked her hair behind that ear that stuck out a little more than the other one. I loved that ear. I never told her. You're supposed to tell people about their ears.

The sliver of street is graying. Or I am. It's hard to tell which of us is leaving first.

*Thump.*

A pause. A long one. I wait for the next with the patience of a man waiting for a door to open, and when it comes it is quieter, farther off, like something walking away down a long hall.

The cobblestones really are warm. I press my cheek to them. A dog barks somewhere—two streets over, three—and I think, *good*, and I don't know why, and then

*thump*

I don't

# The Hamster

Detective Sarah Chen had been working homicides for eleven years. She'd seen what adults did to each other in the dark corners of the city. But standing in the pink-wallpapered bedroom of 1247 Maple Street, she felt something she hadn't felt in a long time.

Cold.

The note was folded neatly on the desk, placed between a spelling test marked with a gold star and a half-finished drawing of a unicorn. Block letters. Careful. The kind of handwriting a teacher praises.

She pulled on fresh gloves before picking it up.

---

*Dear Mr. Whiskers,*

*I am sorry I had to do it but you wouldn't stop looking at me. Mommy says when something looks at you too long it's because it knows what you are thinking. I didn't want you to know.*

*I tried other things first. I tried not feeding you so you would be too tired to look. I tried covering the cage with my blanket but I could still feel you looking through it. I could feel it in my teeth.*

*I read in a book that you have to be quick so they don't feel it. I was quick. I counted to three like when I jump in the pool. One. Two. Three. I wasn't even scared.*

*The part that was surprising was how warm you stayed. I thought you would get cold right away but you didn't. I held you for a long time after. I think that was the nicest part of knowing you.*

*I buried you by the roses because Mommy said roses like things that used to be alive.*

*I feel much better now. I can sleep again. But now the goldfish is looking at me.*

*Love,*
*Emma*

---

Chen read it twice. Then a third time, slower.

Downstairs, she could hear the mother crying in the kitchen, explaining to the uniforms that Emma was *such a good girl, straight A's, never any trouble, please, there must be some mistake about the babysitter—*

Chen looked at the drawing of the unicorn. It was good. Really good, for a nine-year-old. The horn was shaded carefully, the mane flowing in a wind that wasn't there.

In the bottom corner, almost hidden in the grass, Emma had drawn a small pile of what might have been flowers.

Or might not.

Chen slipped the note into an evidence bag and walked to the window. The rose garden was visible from here. Beautiful, full blooms. The healthiest on the block, according to the neighbor who'd called it in after seeing what Emma had done to the Hendersons' cat.

The steel door buckled on the second kick, and Kasia shouldered through with the nozzle already hissing.

The pilot light was a small blue tongue at the end of the wand, polite as a birthday candle. She squeezed the trigger and it became something else entirely — a roaring orange throat that swallowed the doorway and vomited into the room beyond.

The heat hit back. That was the thing people never told you about flame projectors: the air came back at you, a wall of it, shoving against her visor and drying her eyeballs through the slit of her mask. Sweat sprang out on her neck and was gone in the same breath, cooked off before it could run. Inside the suit she was already swimming.

Men had been waiting behind the overturned table. They stood up into the fire the way swimmers come up for air, and then they were running, and then they were falling, and the running ones were worse. One of them went full tilt into the far wall and slid down it leaving a black smear, still trying to beat at his sleeves with hands that no longer worked like hands.

The screaming started late. It always did. The lungs needed a second to understand.

The smell came through the filter anyway. Nothing stopped it — she'd tried charcoal, tried menthol under the nose, tried holding her breath until her vision purpled. It got in. Pork fat in a skillet, and burnt hair, and underneath both of those a sweetness like caramel left too long on the stove. That was the part that stayed with you. Days later you'd be eating something in a roadside cafe and your stomach would turn over for no reason at all, and you'd know why.

She swept the wand left to right, economical, the way her instructor had taught her a lifetime ago. Don't paint. Don't linger. A half-second was a sentence; a full second was a paragraph; anything longer was just indulgence, and indulgence cost fuel.

One of them made it almost to her boots. He was on his knees, and his mouth was open, and whatever he was trying to say came out only as sound. She stepped back once, not from squeamishness — there was no time for squeamishness — but because his jacket was spitting droplets of something molten and she didn't want it on her greaves.

Then the room was quiet except for the fire itself, which muttered and cracked and went about its work.

Kasia eased off the trigger. The blue pilot returned, small and mannered. She counted the shapes on the floor, matched the count to the contract, and keyed her throat mic.

"Room's clear," she said. "Tell the client he can pay the rest now."

She stepped back into the corridor before the sprinklers came on, because she hated getting wet almost as much as she hated the smell.

# The Unmaking of Eliza Vance

The first thing Eliza noticed was the itch—not on her skin, but beneath it. A crawling, scrabbling sensation, as though something small and patient had taken up residence in the hollow between muscle and bone.

She scratched until she bled. The blood came out too dark, too slow, clotting into strange geometries on her fingertips.

---

The shedding began on a Tuesday.

She woke to find her pillowcase dusted with translucent flakes, long curling strips like birch bark peeled from her forearms in the night. Beneath, the new skin gleamed pale and waxen, threaded with veins that pulsed in rhythms her heart did not recognize. She told herself it was eczema. Stress. The late autumn dryness.

By Thursday, sheets of it were sloughing from her shoulders, her thighs, the soft skin behind her knees. She gathered the discarded husks and burned them in the kitchen sink, watching the smoke curl in ways that almost—*almost*—suggested a face.

---

The bones came next.

It started as a deep ache in her jaw, a grinding pressure that made her molars feel loose in their sockets. Then one morning, looking in the mirror, she watched her own cheekbone shift beneath the skin—a slow migration, as though the skull remembered a different architecture it preferred. She felt the *pop* of her collarbone lengthening. The wet crackle of ribs widening to accommodate something her lungs had not yet grown into.

The pain was terrible. She found, increasingly, that she did not mind it.

Her fingers stretched in the night. Her spine rearranged itself in increments—each vertebra renegotiating its relationship to the next—until she stood half an inch taller, then an inch, then two. Her hips cracked like ice on a frozen pond. When she walked, she walked wrongly, with a gait that was not hers, that belonged to something that had never needed to pretend.

---

The last thing to go was the part of her that cared.

She noticed it first in small absences. The neighbor's cat, hit by a car, twitching in the gutter—she watched it die with the detached interest of someone observing weather. A coworker wept at her desk, and Eliza felt only a thin curiosity about the salt content of tears, the inefficiency of grief.

The guardrails went one by one. Guilt went first; it had always been the most tiresome. Then empathy, which had required such constant maintenance. Shame dissolved like sugar in warm water. What remained was appetite—clean, uncomplicated, honest in a way her old self had never managed to be.

She began to understand that the morality she'd worn had been another kind of skin. Thin. Provisional. Something grown over the true shape of her to make her palatable to a world that now seemed very small, and very soft, and very full of things that could be taken.

---

On the final night, Eliza Vance stood before the mirror and did not recognize herself. This did not trouble her. Recognition, she understood now, was for creatures who needed to be known.

She smiled with a mouth that held too many teeth, and went out into the dark to see what the dark had been saving for her.

# The Last Five Minutes

*A small room. A metal door. A man in gray coveralls sits on a bench, hands cuffed in his lap. Another man in a dark uniform leans against the wall opposite him, checking his watch.*

---

**EXECUTIONER:** You want water? I can get you water.

**PRISONER:** Third time you've asked.

**EXECUTIONER:** Protocol.

**PRISONER:** No it isn't.

*A pause.*

**EXECUTIONER:** No. It isn't.

**PRISONER:** How long you been doing this?

**EXECUTIONER:** Eleven years.

**PRISONER:** How many?

**EXECUTIONER:** I don't count.

**PRISONER:** Yes you do.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(quietly)* Twenty-three.

**PRISONER:** Huh.

**EXECUTIONER:** What?

**PRISONER:** Thought it'd be more.

*The Executioner almost laughs. Catches himself.*

**EXECUTIONER:** Chaplain's outside if you changed your mind.

**PRISONER:** I didn't.

**EXECUTIONER:** Alright.

*Silence. The Prisoner studies his cuffed hands.*

**PRISONER:** Can I ask you something?

**EXECUTIONER:** Sure.

**PRISONER:** You think I did it?

**EXECUTIONER:** Not my job to think that.

**PRISONER:** That's not what I asked.

*The Executioner looks at him for a long moment.*

**EXECUTIONER:** Doesn't matter what I think.

**PRISONER:** It does to me. Right now. In this room. It does.

*A long silence.*

**EXECUTIONER:** I read the file.

**PRISONER:** Everybody read the file.

**EXECUTIONER:** I read it twice.

**PRISONER:** And?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(after a beat)* I think a lot of things. I think it doesn't help either of us if I say them out loud.

**PRISONER:** That's a coward's answer.

**EXECUTIONER:** Yeah. It probably is.

*The Prisoner nods slowly, accepting this. The Executioner checks his watch again.*

**PRISONER:** Three minutes?

**EXECUTIONER:** About that.

**PRISONER:** My mother's out there.

**EXECUTIONER:** I know.

**PRISONER:** She made a peach cobbler last Sunday. They let her bring it. Wasn't even her recipe — she got it off the back of a Bisquick box in '78. She's been making it wrong for forty years.

**EXECUTIONER:** Was it good?

**PRISONER:** Best thing I ever ate.

*The Executioner looks at the floor.*

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm sorry.

**PRISONER:** For what part?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(after a long pause)* All of it. The part I do. The part I don't.

**PRISONER:** You gonna sleep tonight?

**EXECUTIONER:** No.

**PRISONER:** Good.

*The Executioner nods. He doesn't take offense.*

**EXECUTIONER:** It's time.

**PRISONER:** Okay.

*The Prisoner stands. He's steady. The Executioner moves to the door, then stops.*

**EXECUTIONER:** For what it's worth — I read it twice because the second time I was hoping I'd see something different.

**PRISONER:** Did you?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(opening the door)* I saw a man.

*They walk out together.*

---

The first handful sounded like rain.

That was what Elena thought, in the soft gray moment before her mind caught up to her body. Rain on a roof. She was a child again, listening to storms from her grandmother's attic bed, safe beneath the quilts.

Then the second handful landed, and the third, and her mind snapped into place like a bone resetting.

Dark. Complete dark. The kind that pressed against her eyes, that made her wonder if her eyes were even open, until she blinked and felt her lashes brush wood.

Wood.

Six inches above her face.

She tried to sit up and her forehead struck the lid with a dull, meaty sound. Pain bloomed white behind her eyes. She tried to turn her head and her ears scraped against the sides. Her shoulders were pinned. Her hands, when she tried to lift them, met a ceiling just above her chest.

The scream started somewhere below her ribs and tore its way out of her, and the sound had nowhere to go. It hit the lid and came back into her mouth, hot and useless. She screamed again and the air she had just spent was gone, and she had to suck it back in, and there was less of it now, she was sure of it, there had to be less—

*Thud.*

More dirt. Heavier now. A shovelful, not a handful. Someone was working in a rhythm up there.

*Thud.*

She clawed at the lid. Her fingernails bent backward and she felt one tear loose at the quick, and she didn't care, she scrabbled until splinters drove into the pads of her fingers. The wood didn't give. Of course it didn't give. It was built not to give. It was built for exactly this, to hold a body still forever, and her body was still inside it, still and small and alive, and no one knew.

*Thud. Thud.*

Her breath came fast and shallow and she tried to slow it, tried to remember what she'd read once — panic uses oxygen, panic kills you faster — but knowing a thing and doing a thing were different countries, and she could not cross the border. Her lungs pulled and pulled. The air tasted of her own mouth, of cedar, of something older underneath — the dry, patient smell of earth.

*Thud.*

The sound was changing. That was the worst of it, somehow. At first each shovelful had rung against the lid with a bright, percussive slap. Now the slaps were muffling. Softening. Each layer of dirt buried the sound of the next, the way snow quiets a street. She was listening to herself disappear.

She pressed her palms flat against the lid and pushed. Pushed with everything, with the long muscles of her arms and the desperate hinge of her shoulders, and the wood groaned — it *groaned* — and for one incandescent second she believed. Then it held. Then it settled back against her, heavier, because now there was weight on it, weight that hadn't been there a minute ago, and there would only be more.

*Thud.*

She turned her face to the side, cheek against the lining, and a tear ran sideways into her ear. She had not known she was crying. She whispered her own name, to prove she was still the person she had been that morning — Elena, Elena, Elena — and her breath fogged the wood an inch from her lips, and she could feel that fog, she could feel her own warmth coming back at her, and that was when she understood how small the world had become.

The shovels above her kept their rhythm.

*Thud.*

Softer.

*Thud.*

Softer still.

And then she could not hear them at all, and that was somehow worse than hearing them, because silence meant the dirt was deep enough now to swallow sound, and she was alone down here with the slow arithmetic of her own breathing, subtracting itself, one shallow gasp at a time, from a number she had never been allowed to know.

# The Conversion Wing

The corridor smelled of antiseptic and something else—something organic and wrong, like meat left too long in sunlight. Elena pressed her forehead against the cold tile floor of her cell and tried to remember her mother's face. The image came in fragments now: a curve of jaw, the suggestion of dark eyes. Three weeks in Processing had already begun eating her memories, and she hadn't even reached the tables yet.

They came for her at the hour without name. The hour when the lights in the cells hummed at a frequency that made teeth ache. Two Converted orderlies—what had once been men, perhaps—walked on legs that bent the wrong way, their eyes replaced with glass apertures that clicked as they focused. One of them had been her neighbor, Tomás, who used to play chess in the plaza. She knew by the old scar on his wrist. He did not know her.

The operating theater was white. Brutally, impossibly white, as though color itself had been declared subversive. She was strapped to a table that was warm with the body heat of whoever had lain there before her. Above her, the surgical array descended—a blossom of instruments, each polished to a mirror finish, so she could watch herself disappear.

There was no anesthesia. The State had determined, in one of its efficiency reports, that consciousness during conversion improved neural integration. Pain was a teaching tool. Pain was how the body learned to accept its new purposes.

The first incision ran from sternum to navel. Elena heard herself scream, but the sound seemed to come from very far away, from someone she used to be. They were already working inside her, threading cold filaments along her spine, replacing the soft architecture of her lungs with bellows of synthetic muscle and mesh. Each nerve they touched sang a different note of agony. She learned, in those hours, that pain had colors. That it had geography. That there were territories within her body she had never visited, and now they were all burning.

She tried to hold onto things. Her grandmother's lullaby. The taste of oranges. The name of the boy she had kissed behind the library when she was seventeen. But each time the instruments descended, another small room inside her went dark. They were not just reshaping her flesh—they were editing her, excising whatever parts of her soul could not be made useful.

When she woke—if waking was the word—she could feel the new weight of her jaw, the servos that would now shape her speech into the clipped syllables of compliance. Her hands had been given precision she had never asked for. Somewhere in her chest, a small reactor hummed contentedly, and she knew with terrible certainty that she would never again feel cold, or hunger, or the particular warmth of being held.

She was led to a mirror. The thing that looked back at her was beautiful in the way that weapons are beautiful. Its face held the topography of Elena, but her eyes were gone—replaced with those same clicking apertures. When she tried to cry, no tears came. The ducts had been deemed inefficient.

Inside, somewhere very deep, the last small human part of her was screaming. It would keep screaming, she understood, for the rest of her functional life. But the scream would never reach her face. Her face belonged to the State now. Her hands belonged to the State. Her breath, measured and perfect, belonged to the State.

Only the screaming was still hers.

And even that, she suspected, they would find a way to take.

# The Composition

Dr. Ellis Vance had been photographing crime scenes for nineteen years before she admitted, even to herself, that some of them were beautiful.

The admission had come slowly, the way frost creeps across a window. First it was just a noticing: the way blood pooled in concentric rings on a hardwood floor, obeying the same physics as a Rothko bleed. Then the noticing became a waiting. She would arrive at scenes hoping—though she never used that word, not even in her private thoughts—that this one would have *something* to it. A geometry. A gesture.

Her colleagues assumed her long silences at scenes were professional rigor. In truth, she was composing. Reading.

The Hartley scene, in the autumn of her forty-third year, was the one she knew she would never forgive herself for loving.

The victim had been arranged—there was no other word—in the conservatory of a Federal-style house on Chestnut Street. Morning light came through the leaded glass in long, honeyed parallelograms. The body lay on its side in the center of the tiled floor, one arm extended, the fingers slightly curled as though reaching for something just out of frame. A single white camellia had been placed beside the open palm.

Ellis stood in the doorway and did not breathe for a long moment.

It was the *restraint* of it that undid her. There was so little blood. A thin dark line traced from the corner of the mouth to the ear and stopped there, precise as a calligrapher's stroke. The victim's pale robe had fallen open just enough to suggest vulnerability without vulgarity. The hair had been smoothed. Someone—the killer, she understood with a cold certainty—had arranged the hair.

The tile beneath the body was a pattern of black and white diamonds, and the body had been placed so that the reaching hand bisected exactly one diamond, dividing black from white along the line of the wrist. Ellis noted this. She noted, too, that the camellia had been set not at random but at the vanishing point of the conservatory's perspective, so that anyone entering from the main door—as she had—was drawn to it as inevitably as to the center of a Vermeer.

*He wants me to see*, she thought, and then corrected herself, because she did not know it was a he, and because the thought had been dangerous in a different way: *He wants me to see what he saw.*

She knelt. She took her photographs. She measured. She did all of the things a forensic investigator does, and she did them with the hollow competence of someone performing a ritual whose meaning has been replaced by another, secret meaning.

When she was alone for a moment—the uniforms outside, the coroner's van not yet arrived—she did something she had never done before. She took a photograph with her own phone. Just one. Framed the way she would have framed it if she had been the one to stage the body, if the conservatory had been her canvas.

That night, in her apartment, she opened the image on her laptop and looked at it for a long time with a glass of wine going warm in her hand. She thought about the camellia. She thought about the diamond of tile bisected by the wrist. She thought about how the light must have been different an hour earlier, and an hour later, and how the killer had chosen the hour that he had.

She thought: *I could find him.*

And beneath that thought, quieter, the one that frightened her:

*I could find him, and I could ask him how he learned to see.*

She closed the laptop. She did not delete the photograph. She poured another glass of wine and sat in the dark, waiting for morning, when she would return to the scene and try, one more time, to look at it the way a person is supposed to look at such things—with horror, with pity, with the clean professional distance that had been her armor for nineteen years.

She already knew the armor would not fit her anymore. It had been tailored for a woman who had not yet seen the camellia.

Outside, the city went about its ordinary violence. Somewhere in it, she understood, he was also awake, also thinking about the composition, also waiting to see what she would make of his gift.

She found she was smiling, very slightly, and could not remember when she had begun.

# The Hanging Tree

The cottonwood had seen this work before. Its thickest branch ran out parallel to the hardpan like it had been shaped by the Almighty for exactly this purpose, the bark worn smooth in one particular spot where rope had bitten deep across the years.

Hollis Crane sat the borrowed mare with his hands bound behind him, hat gone, hair matted to his forehead with sweat that wouldn't stop coming despite the cold. The noose itched. That was the thing nobody told you about hanging — the damn rope itched worse than lice, rough hemp scratching raw at the soft skin under the jaw.

Sheriff Dawes rolled a cigarette one-handed, the paper trembling not at all. "You got words, Hollis, say 'em now."

"I didn't kill that boy."

"You said."

"Dawes—"

"Said your piece." The sheriff licked the paper, sealed it, struck a lucifer off his saddle horn. "Reverend ain't coming. You want to make your peace, make it quiet."

Hollis looked up through the yellowing leaves. A jay was screaming somewhere back in the brush, indignant about something that had nothing to do with the men below it. The sky was that hard blue you only got in November, blue like enamelware.

"Lord," he started, and then couldn't think of what came after.

Dawes nodded at the deputy. The deputy slapped the mare's haunch.

She bolted forward and Hollis dropped.

The sound was not what the dime novels promised. It was a wet green-wood *crack*, the noise of a fence rail giving under too much weight, muffled by meat. His head canted hard to the left, chin nearly meeting his shoulder, and the rope creaked once, a long slow complaint from the branch above.

Then the body began to move.

His boots kicked — not running, not struggling, just the dumb animal jerk of nerves that hadn't gotten the news yet. One knee drew up. Straightened. Drew up again. His bound hands opened and closed behind him like he was trying to catch something falling. A dark stain spread down the front of his trousers. The rope turned him slowly in a half-circle, then back, then a quarter more, as if the tree were looking him over from every side before accepting him.

Dawes drew on his cigarette. The smoke went up straight in the still air.

The twitching eased. A finger moved. Stopped. Moved again. Stopped for good.

"Cut him down in an hour," the sheriff said. "Wire his brother in Ellsworth. Tell him plain."

The deputy was young and hadn't watched one before. He was looking at a spot on the ground about three feet left of the boots.

"Son," Dawes said, not unkindly. "Look at him. You don't look now, you'll see him every night you close your eyes. Look at him till he's just a thing hanging there. That's the trick of it."

The deputy looked.

Above them, the jay finally shut up, and the only sound was the slow, patient creak of the rope turning against the branch — a sound the cottonwood knew by heart.

**The Alley**

Mira had taken this shortcut a hundred times. Tonight, the streetlamp at the far end flickered once and died, and the dark folded over her like a wet coat.

She didn't hear him arrive. That was the thing that would haunt the last clear minute of her mind—no footstep, no breath, only the sudden wrongness of not being alone. When she turned, he was already close enough to touch.

Elias had not fed in four nights.

The hunger was not a feeling anymore; it had become weather. It moved through him in slow, grinding tides, hollowing the spaces behind his ribs, drawing his jaw tight until his teeth ached at their roots. He had walked past a butcher's window an hour ago and nearly gone to his knees at the smell of old blood on sawdust. Now, with a living pulse two feet away, the world narrowed to the blue flutter at the side of her throat—that small, stupid, beautiful muscle beating out its little alarm.

"Don't," he said, and he wasn't sure if he was speaking to her or to himself.

She tried to run. He caught her wrist without seeming to move, and the bones there felt like a bird's, hot through the skin. He pressed her gently back against the brick. Gentleness was the last cruelty he could still afford her.

"Look at me."

She looked. He held her eyes and let the old weight settle behind his own, and watched her pupils widen, soften, go slack as water. Her shoulders eased from her ears. The scream she had been building unmade itself in her throat.

"It won't hurt long," he whispered, and meant it.

He tilted her head. Her scarf slipped. The vein was right there, a faint blue road under pale skin, and he felt his mouth change—the ache of the fangs descending, that private humiliation, that relief. He bent to her neck the way a penitent bends to an altar.

The puncture was two small, precise things. A pressure, then a giving, then heat. Twin points, no wider than sewing needles at the skin, opening into the dark beneath. She made a sound—not pain, only surprise, the soft *oh* of someone who has missed a step on a staircase.

Then the taste.

He had forgotten, between feedings, how bright it was. Iron and salt and something sweeter underneath—the living note, the thing that separated her from meat. It flooded his tongue and every hollow place in him filled by degrees, warm, warm, unbearably warm. His hands at her shoulders steadied, no longer trembling. His vision sharpened until he could count the grains of mortar in the brick beside her cheek.

Mira's knees went first.

She felt it as a puzzling lightness, as though someone had taken a heavy coat off her and she hadn't realized she'd been wearing one. Her fingers, which had been gripping his coat, loosened and slid. The cold of the alley seemed very far away now, held off by a drowsy warmth that rose from her chest into her jaw. She thought, with a strange clarity, of her grandmother's kitchen, of sun on a linoleum floor. She thought she should be frightened. She couldn't quite remember why.

Her heartbeat—he listened to it the way a musician listens to a tempo—was slowing. Still strong, but the gaps between beats were lengthening, each thud a little further from its neighbor. Her breath came shallower against his ear. Her weight, which she had been holding, she gave to him.

*Enough.*

The word arrived from some older, quieter room in him, the one he kept locked most nights. *Enough. Enough now.*

He held on for one more swallow. Two. The hunger, satisfied, had become something worse—greed, which knew no natural stopping point, which would drink her empty and look for more. He had buried people who had misjudged that line. He had been the one burying.

He pulled back.

The first cut came without warning.

Mara had been running for maybe ninety seconds—long enough that the cold air had carved a raw channel down her throat, not long enough to outpace whatever was behind her. She knew this because she could hear it breathing. Not loud. Worse than loud. A patient, interested sound, like something smelling a wound before it decided where to bite.

Then her shoulder opened.

That was how it felt—not *struck*, not *slashed*, but *opened*, the way you'd split a seam. A line of cold drew itself from her collarbone down to her bicep, and for one suspended second there was no pain, only the clean wrong feeling of her skin parting and the air reaching places air was never meant to reach. She looked down and saw the blood before she felt the cut. Her jacket hung in two halves. Beneath it, a neat red mouth, already filling.

The pain arrived a heartbeat later, and it arrived *with interest*, bright and electric, and she heard herself make a sound she didn't recognize.

She kept running.

The woods were empty. That was the obscenity of it. No shape moved between the trees. No shadow lengthened wrong. Twice she spun, gasping, scanning the tree line for something—anything—a silhouette, a distortion, a held breath—and there was only the white afternoon and her own ragged puffs of steam and the absolute, attentive stillness of being watched by nothing.

The second cut took the back of her calf.

Her leg folded. She went down into wet leaves, and the smell of dirt and iron came up to meet her face. She tried to crawl. Something stepped—she heard it, the soft compression of loam under a weight that had no business having weight—and then a third line drew itself across her back, almost gentle, almost thoughtful, the way a butcher might score a cut before committing to it.

That was what broke her. Not the pain. The *consideration* in it. The sense that she was being measured. Tasted. That the thing behind her had all afternoon, and knew it, and was drawing out the question of where, exactly, to open her next.

She pressed her forehead to the cold ground and listened to it breathe.

It was very close now.

It smelled, faintly, of her own blood—as if it had already been inside her and was only now getting around to the rest.

# The Weight

The room smelled of copper and kerosene. Dust motes drifted through the slant of light from the single high window, indifferent as stars.

They had tied Mara to the chair on the left. Dren to the chair on the right. Between them, on the concrete floor marked by the ghosts of older stains, they had set a stool for Kova to sit on. A courtesy, the commander had called it. *Sit. Think. Choose.*

Mara was not crying. That was the worst of it. Mara, who cried at weddings and stubbed toes and the end of sad films, sat with her jaw set like a stone wall. Her eyes kept finding Kova's and sliding away, as though afraid to ask for anything.

Dren was shaking. A fine tremor that ran through him like current through a wire. He'd bitten through his lip sometime in the last hour, and a dark thread ran down his chin into his collar. When he caught Kova looking, he tried to smile. The smile collapsed halfway.

"Five minutes," the commander said, from somewhere behind the lamp.

Kova's mind was a drowning thing. It kept surfacing on irrelevancies. The time Dren had carried him six kilometers on a ruined ankle. The way Mara laughed with her whole ribcage. Her sister, waiting somewhere. His sister, waiting somewhere. A kettle left on a stove in a house that no longer existed.

*Choose one, and the other lives. Refuse, and we shoot both.*

He tried the math of it the way a man tries doorknobs in a burning house. Mara had the child. Dren had the skills they needed for the road ahead. Mara would forgive him. Dren would forgive him. Neither forgiveness would matter because the one he named would be past forgiving. He would be the last thing they saw — his mouth shaping their name.

He thought: *I could say my own.* He opened his mouth to say it and the commander, who had heard this before from better men, only laughed softly and said, "No. That one isn't on the table."

"Three minutes."

Kova's hands were wet. He hadn't known a person could sweat from the palms like that, like something was trying to get out of him through the skin.

Mara spoke first. Her voice was level, almost gentle, as though she were coaxing a frightened animal. "Kova. Look at me." He couldn't. "Kova. Say my name."

"Don't," Dren whispered. "Don't make him —"

"Say my name, Kova."

He looked at her. Her eyes were wet now, finally, but her face was still that stone wall, and he understood that she was giving him something. She was taking the choice and placing it in his mouth like a coin, so that all he had to do was let it fall.

"Mara," he said.

It came out a crack, a splinter of sound. She nodded once, as if he'd answered a question about the weather.

"Good," she said. "Good. It's alright."

Dren made a sound that wasn't a word.

The commander stepped forward, and the world contracted to the small black circle of the barrel and the great white circle of Mara's face, and Kova heard himself saying *wait, wait,* though he knew there was no waiting, there had never been waiting, the waiting had ended the moment they came through the door that morning —

The shot was louder than any shot he had ever heard, though he had heard many. It was louder because it was inside his chest.

Mara's head did not fly back the way it did in films. It simply dropped, as if something holding her up had been untied. A dark blossom opened above her eyebrow and another, worse, behind, and the wall behind her chair received what the wall received, and the light through the high window went on being indifferent.

Dren was screaming. Kova realized he was screaming too. Their screams braided together in the small room and went nowhere.

They cut Dren loose. They left Mara where she was. They pushed Kova, stumbling, past her chair, and he did not look, and then he did look, because not-looking would have been another betrayal and he had used up his allowance of those for one life.

Her eyes were half-open. Her mouth was soft. She did not look peaceful. People who say the dead look peaceful have not seen enough of them. She looked like a person interrupted.

Outside, the daylight was an obscenity. Dren was on his knees in the dirt, retching. Kova stood above him and felt the sun on his face and understood, with a clarity that would never leave him, that he had survived, and that surviving was the punishment, and that he would carry Mara's name in his mouth like the coin she had put there until the day someone closed his jaw for the last time.

He knelt down beside Dren and put his hand on his friend's shaking back, and neither of them spoke, because there were no words yet invented for what had just been done, and the old words — *friend*, *choice*, *mercy* — were ruined now, and would have to be remade, or abandoned, or carried like the dead are carried: heavily, and without ceremony, and for a very long way.

# The Cellar Door

Martin had only gone next door to return the hedge trimmers.

Dave wasn't home—his truck was gone, and the back door hung open, swinging lazily in the October wind. Martin called out twice. No answer. He stepped inside with the trimmers, intending to leave them on the kitchen counter with a note.

That's when he smelled it.

Not rot, exactly. Something chemical beneath something organic. Bleach layered over meat left too long in a cooler. It seeped up through the floorboards from somewhere below.

Martin's stomach knotted. Dave had always been *off*—too friendly, too quick with a smile, the kind of man who remembered the names of your kids but not in a warm way. In a cataloguing way.

The basement door was open a crack. Martin told himself he was being ridiculous. He told himself he should leave. Instead, his hand found the knob, and he pulled.

The stairs creaked under his weight. A single bulb glowed at the bottom, yellow and sick. He reached the concrete floor and stopped.

The room had been finished—drywall, shelves, a workbench. It looked, at first glance, like any hobbyist's den. Then his eyes adjusted to what he was actually seeing.

Rows of mason jars lined the shelves, each labeled in careful black marker with a name and a date. Some contained locks of hair coiled like sleeping snakes. Others held rings, driver's licenses, a child's barrette. One jar, near the back, held a single molar with the root still attached.

On the workbench lay a ledger, open, filled with Dave's tidy handwriting—dates, locations, and beside each, a small notation Martin couldn't bring himself to read twice.

Above the bench hung a corkboard covered in photographs. Women. Men. A girl who couldn't have been more than nineteen, smiling at a camera she didn't know was watching.

Martin's knees nearly gave. He gripped the workbench to steady himself, and that's when he saw the chest freezer in the corner, humming quietly, a padlock hanging open from its hasp.

He did not open it. Later, he would tell the detectives he didn't need to. He already knew.

What he did was back slowly up the stairs, hands trembling so hard he dropped the trimmers twice. He walked—did not run, because running felt like it might summon something—across the lawn to his own kitchen. He locked the door. He called 911.

Then he sat at his kitchen table, looking out the window at Dave's tidy house with its well-kept garden and cheerful wreath on the door, and he waited for the sirens.

They arrived in four minutes.

Dave's truck pulled into the driveway in six.

---

# Lockdown

The alarm hit first—a flat, pulsing wail that swallowed every other sound in C-Block. Then the lights cut to emergency red, and the corridor became a tunnel of blood-colored shadow.

Officer Reyes saw it start from the mezzanine: a tray sailing across the dayroom, catching a guard across the temple. The guard's knees buckled the way knees do when the brain goes dark for a second. Before he hit the tile, three inmates were on him.

"Code Black, C-Block, Code Black—"

Her radio dissolved into static and shouting. Somewhere below, a plexiglass panel spiderwebbed under repeated blows from a weight-room dumbbell someone had smuggled past the sweep. A table went over. Then another. Men who had spent years measuring each other now collapsed those measurements into fists and elbows and sharpened toothbrushes pulled from waistbands.

Reyes slammed the gate release for the upper tier, trying to contain the spread, but a inmate named Vasquez—she knew him, he'd been quiet for eight years—had already wedged a mop handle into the track. The gate shuddered and stopped half-closed. Men squeezed through sideways, grinning with the terrible clarity of people who had decided not to be afraid anymore.

# Clean Work

The hotel room smelled like gun oil and room service coffee. Marcus had the bedspread covered in newspaper — old habit from his father, who'd been a mechanic, not an assassin, but the principle was the same. Don't get oil on things you have to pay for.

"Piano wire," Vera said from the desk, where she was disassembling a Beretta with the patient precision of someone folding laundry. "Nothing beats it."

"Piano wire is theatrical."

"Piano wire is *elegant*."

"Piano wire means you have to get close enough to smell what they had for lunch." Marcus ran a bore snake through the barrel of his rifle. "I'll stay three hundred yards away, thanks."

"Of course you will. You're a coward."

"I'm a professional."

"You're a coward *professionally*." She held the slide up to the lamp, squinting at it. "Pass the solvent?"

He slid the bottle across the carpet with his foot. She caught it without looking.

"Snipers never have to look anyone in the eye," she continued. "It's like — what's the word. Parasocial. You're having a parasocial relationship with your targets."

"That is aggressively not what parasocial means."

"It's what it means when I say it."

Marcus shook his head and worked a patch through the chamber. Outside, somewhere below them, a car alarm went off and then gave up halfway through its cycle, like it had thought better of the whole thing.

"Fine," he said. "What about you? You don't have a favorite?"

"I told you. Piano wire."

"No, come on. Really."

Vera was quiet for a moment, laying out the Beretta's parts in a neat line: slide, barrel, recoil spring, frame. Like place settings at a dinner party.

"A long walk," she said finally.

"What does that mean?"

"Exactly what I said. A long walk. You get them somewhere quiet, somewhere they're not expecting anything, and you just — walk with them. Talk to them. Let them have the walk." She shrugged. "Then at the end of it, whatever. Doesn't matter how. The walk is the thing."

Marcus looked up from his rifle.

"That's horrifying, Vera."

"You asked."

"That's genuinely the worst thing anyone's ever told me."

"You shoot people from rooftops like you're playing a video game and *I'm* horrifying."

"Yes."

She laughed — a real laugh, surprised out of her — and went back to her pistol.

The television was on with the sound off. Some cooking show. A man in a white coat was yelling silently at a younger man in a white coat, who looked like he was about to cry into a pot of something.

"What time's the thing," Marcus said.

"Four."

"Plenty of time."

"Plenty of time."

He reached for the oil. She reached for the coffee. On the TV, the younger chef finally cried.

The pyre catches slowly at first. Green wood hisses before it surrenders to flame, and she feels the heat as a living thing—first a warmth against her shins like standing too close to a hearth, then something insistent, pressing, climbing her skirts. By the time the fire finds the pitch-soaked kindling beneath her feet, the warmth has become a presence that scours. Her skin tightens, then splits. The air above the flames shimmers and distorts the faces of the crowd into something fluid and unreal, as though she is already seeing them from the other side of the world.

The smoke is what takes her first, and this is a mercy the executioners sometimes allowed and sometimes denied. Damp straw and pine resin make a grey-black column that bends in the wind and stings the eyes of those who came to watch. It fills her lungs with a taste like burnt tar and iron, and she coughs until she cannot cough, and her head falls forward against the iron collar that holds her to the post. Her hair has already gone—a brief bright crown, then nothing. Ash catches in the mouths of the watching children. Somewhere a dog is barking.

Her screams, when they come, are not the operatic cries of a stage death. They are smaller and more terrible than that—a thin, animal sound from a throat scorched raw, half-swallowed by smoke. She calls for her mother, who has been dead eleven years. She calls for God, in the plain voice of someone who has always called for Him and expects to be heard. Then only a rasping, and then the fire speaks for her, popping and roaring, and the priest intones his Latin a little louder to cover what cannot quite be covered.

When it is over, the crowd disperses in near silence. A woman wipes her child's face. The smell will be in their clothes for days.

# The Raising at Thornhollow

The necromancer Veyra Kell stood ankle-deep in mud that had once been a wheat field, now churned black by three days of rain and the deeper work that was coming. Around her, the pauper's pits yawned open, their shallow graves disgorging the plague-dead of the last hard winter.

She began with the old invocation, though *invocation* was a gentle word for what the syllables did to the air. They didn't travel outward—they pulled inward, dragging warmth and sound and the small comforting noises of the world into her throat. A nightjar stopped mid-call and never finished. The rain itself faltered for a heartbeat, droplets hanging like beads on a drawn thread before remembering gravity.

The magic was wrong, and she felt it as she always did: a nausea that lived behind her teeth. Proper sorcery had shape. It had edges, grammar, a kind of music. This had *none* of that. It was a slow unpeeling of the veil between what should stay buried and what she needed. Every cantrip was a small blasphemy, and she had strung a thousand of them together tonight like pearls on a string of hair.

The first hand broke the soil.

It was a woman's hand, or had been—the skin the color of wet parchment, fingers swollen at the knuckles, the nails gone soft and lifting like wet petals. A ring still clung to the index finger, grown too small for the bloated flesh. The body that followed was worse: belly distended with gas that had not finished its work, a face slack and running, the lower jaw hanging by one string of tendon. When Veyra's magic found the hollow where a soul had been, the corpse's eyes opened, and there was nothing behind them. Not hunger, not rage, not even the dreadful curiosity some of the freshly dead wore. Just the same flat, wet gleam as stagnant water.

It stood. Stood *wrongly*—hinging at joints that had softened past utility, held upright by her will alone, a puppet with half its strings cut and the rest tied to her ribs.

Then the others.

They came up from the mud in groups of three and four, because the pits had been dug in haste and the dead had been tipped in together. A boy no older than twelve rose embracing an old man; they did not separate, only turned their ruined faces toward her in unison. A pregnant woman, swollen grotesquely, the curve of her belly moving in a way Veyra did not let herself examine. Soldiers still in rusted mail, the metal fused to what remained of their chests. A priest whose holy medallion had burned a black cross-shape into the bone of his sternum.

They smelled, and it was not simply the smell of death. Death had a clean logic—rot, earth, the sweet-sour of decay. This smelled like death *interrupted*. Like a wound that had been sewn shut over infection. Somewhere in the ranks, a body that had not been ready made a long wet sound as something inside it gave way.

Veyra's hands were shaking. They always shook, this deep into a raising. Part of her—the part trained by her mother in the herbalist's cottage, the part that had loved a man once and buried him properly with coins on his eyes—that part was screaming behind a door she had long ago nailed shut. The door bowed outward tonight. It always did, when there were this many.

Six hundred and forty-one. She had counted the pits.

She raised her hand, and six hundred and forty-one ruined faces turned with the gesture, a field of wet flowers following a black sun. The rain resumed. The nightjar did not.

Somewhere south, the barony of Thornhollow was sleeping, and its lord had not yet learned that burning the plague-dead in the old way—with salt, with cedar, with the prayers spoken backward—was not a superstition.

It was a precaution.

And he had been too cheap to afford it.

Veyra Kell swallowed the taste of her own magic, spat black into the mud, and began to walk south. Her army came with her, silent but for the suck of their feet in the wet earth, and the occasional soft sound of something falling off.

# The Last Supper at Thornwood

Margaret lifted her wine glass, and I watched the crystal catch the candlelight. Three sips. That was all it would take.

"You've outdone yourself, Eleanor," she said, that practiced smile stretching across her face. The same smile she'd worn at the reading of Father's will, when she'd walked away with the estate that should have been mine. "The lamb is exquisite."

"An old recipe of Mother's." I cut into my own portion—from a separate pan, of course. "She always said the secret was in the reduction."

She took another bite, and I counted silently. The foxglove extract was slow. Elegant. It would announce itself in stages.

"Do you remember the summers here?" I asked, refilling her glass myself. "When we were girls?"

"I try not to dwell on the past." She dabbed her lips with linen. "It's a habit you might consider, Ellie."

*Ellie.* She hadn't called me that in twenty years.

The first sign came between the lamb and the salad course. She touched her temple, frowning slightly.

"Are you well?"

"Just a small headache. The wine, perhaps." She laughed, but there was the faintest tremor in it. "I've been working too hard."

I nodded with concern I did not feel. Her pupils had begun to dilate, swallowing the pale blue of her eyes. She reached for her water and I noticed her fingers weren't quite steady on the stem.

"The gardens have bloomed beautifully this year," I said, steering us toward harmless things. "Particularly the foxglove along the south wall."

"Mm." She wasn't really listening. Her other hand had drifted to her chest, pressing lightly, as if checking for something. A flutter. An irregularity.

"Margaret?"

"My heart is—" She paused, swallowed. "It's skipping. Strangely."

"Shall I call someone?"

"No, no. It will pass." But a sheen of sweat had appeared at her hairline, catching the candlelight like tiny pearls. She reached for her wine again, then stopped, staring at the glass. "Everything looks... there's a yellow cast to the room. Is that the candles?"

"Beeswax," I said. "They always burn warm."

She nodded, but slowly, as if her head had grown heavy. The nausea would come next—I saw her swallow twice, three times, her throat working against it. Her color was changing, a waxy paleness blooming under her cheeks.

"Eleanor." Her voice had dropped to something smaller. "I don't feel—"

"You look tired," I said gently. "Why don't you rest a moment?"

She tried to stand. Her legs seemed to belong to someone else. She sat down hard, one hand splayed on the tablecloth, fingers trembling now in earnest.

I poured myself more wine and watched her understand. It came into her eyes slowly, the way dawn comes into a room—first gray, then gold, then terrible.

"Ellie," she whispered.

"Yes," I said. "I know."

Outside, the foxglove along the south wall swayed in the evening breeze, and I sat with my sister for the last time, and finished my meal.

# The Price of Treachery

The sun hung low and bloody over the *Marauder's Grin*, painting the deck in shades of rust and shadow. Captain Mordecai Crane stood with one boot propped on a barrel, the tip of his cutlass tracing lazy circles in the air before the bound man's throat.

"Thomas Ellery," the captain said, voice soft as silk drawn over a blade. "You shared my rum. You ate my salt pork. And then you whispered of mutiny in the dark like a rat in the walls."

Ellery's knees had given out an hour ago. Two crewmen held him upright now, his shirt torn open, sweat cutting tracks through the grime on his face. He was twenty-three years old. He had wanted, more than anything, to see his sister in Bristol again.

"Captain, please—I was drunk, I swear on my mother's grave I didn't mean—"

"Your mother's grave." Crane smiled, and it was a terrible thing. "Then she'll have company soon enough."

The crew had gathered in a silent half-moon. None of them met Ellery's eyes. They had all seen this before, and those who hadn't would learn the lesson today: loyalty was the only coin that spent on Crane's ship.

The plank jutted out over the starboard rail, a weathered length of oak that had seen a dozen such mornings. Below, the water churned strangely. Crane had ordered buckets of chum poured over the side an hour past. The sea had answered.

Grey fins cut the surface in restless circles. Now and then a dark shape rolled, and a white belly flashed, and an eye—flat, black, ancient—considered the ship with the patience of something that had been hunting since before men had learned to build them.

"Walk," Crane said.

Ellery was untied. His legs barely held him. He stumbled toward the plank, and the crew parted for him like he was already a ghost.

"Please," he whispered, to no one, to everyone, to God. "Please."

The wood was warm under his bare feet. He took one step, then another. The plank bowed slightly beneath his weight. He could hear his own heartbeat in his ears, louder than the creaking of the rigging, louder than the wind. At the end of the plank, he stopped. He looked down.

The water boiled.

"I have a sister," he said, and his voice broke. "I have a sister in Bristol. Her name is Mary. Someone—someone tell her—"

"Jump," Crane said, "or I'll put a pistol ball in your spine and you'll drown before they ever reach you. Choose your mercy, boy."

Ellery closed his eyes. He thought of Mary, of the smell of bread in their mother's kitchen, of a girl named Anne he had kissed once behind a tavern in Port Royal. He thought of all the small, bright things he would never have again.

He jumped.

The sea took him with a cold slap, and for one merciful moment there was only the green silence of the deep, the muffled roar of bubbles past his ears. He kicked upward, broke the surface, gasped—

The first strike came from below, and it was like being hit by a cannonball. The impact drove the breath out of him before the pain arrived. Then the pain arrived, and it was a white light behind his eyes, and the water around him bloomed dark.

He screamed. He screamed for his mother. He thrashed, and the thrashing drew them as surely as the blood did. A second shape struck him broadside, and something gave way inside him with a sound he felt more than heard. The sea was red now, red and churning, and he could no longer tell up from down.

On the deck, the crew watched in silence. One of the younger men, a boy of sixteen named Pike, turned away and was sick against the rail. No one mocked him for it. Captain Crane watched with the calm of a man observing the weather.

It was mercifully quick, in the end. The sea closed over the last of it. The fins circled for a while longer, then dispersed, one by one, back into the deep.

Crane turned to his crew. He did not raise his voice. He did not need to.

"Back to work," he said.

And the *Marauder's Grin* sailed on, leaving only a dark stain on the water that the tide would swallow by nightfall, as though Thomas Ellery of Bristol had never existed at all.

# The Weight of Silence

The first night, Elias told himself it was the wind.

The scraping sound beneath the floorboards—rhythmic, patient, like fingernails testing the grain of the wood—couldn't be anything else. He'd buried Thomas deep. Deep enough that the frost couldn't reach him. Deep enough that God Himself would need a shovel.

By the third night, Elias stopped lying to himself.

He sat at the kitchen table, a bottle of whiskey sweating in his grip, watching the lamp flame bend sideways though no window was open. The wick guttered, and in its dying orange light, he saw the wet print of a boot on the floorboards. Just one. Leading from the cellar door to the chair across from him.

"You're not here," he whispered.

*But you put me here,* something answered—not in sound, but in the space behind his teeth. A voice that crawled up from the soft meat of his own throat.

He didn't sleep. He *couldn't*. Every time his eyes closed, he felt the shovel in his hands again, felt the *give* of Thomas's skull the way a rotten pumpkin gives. He'd wake to find himself standing in the yard, barefoot in the mud, staring at the patch of earth beneath the willow. The grass there grew greener than anywhere else. Fat and obscene.

The mirror was the worst of it.

On the seventh day, Elias caught his reflection smiling when he wasn't. On the eighth, the reflection lingered a half-second behind his movements, like a man reluctant to follow orders. On the ninth, his reflection had Thomas's eyes—that milky, flat-stone look they'd had after. Staring from his own face. Judging from inside his own skull.

He smashed the mirror with the whiskey bottle. The shards on the floor each held a different piece of Thomas. An eye here. A blue, waterlogged lip there. A dozen small accusations glittering up at him.

He couldn't eat. Every meal tasted of copper and clay. He poured a glass of water and it came out red, though when his wife—*his poor wife, who noticed nothing, who kissed his graying cheek and asked if he was sleeping well*—drank from the same pitcher, she tasted only water. He began to laugh at odd moments. A dry, rattling laugh that didn't feel like his own.

The guilt was not a feeling. It was a tenant. It had moved into the hollow of his chest and was slowly, methodically, rearranging the furniture. Some nights he could hear it humming—a tuneless, childish sound, the way Thomas used to hum while mending fences.

On the fourteenth night, Elias woke to find Thomas sitting on the edge of the bed.

Not a shadow. Not a trick of the moon. *Thomas.* Pale as tallow, hair still wet with the river they'd walked along that last evening, a dark hollow collapsed above his left temple where the shovel had found its home. He was not angry. That was the terrible thing. He looked at Elias with something worse than hatred.

He looked at him with patience.

"How long?" Elias croaked, tears carving tracks through the grime on his face. "How long will you stay?"

Thomas tilted his ruined head. Water dripped from his jaw onto the quilt, and where it landed, the fabric grew dark and spread like a bloom.

*Until you join me,* the silence said. *And not a moment sooner.*

Elias began to laugh again—that dry, rattling laugh—and this time it did not stop. It went on until the dawn came gray and cold through the window, until his wife found him on the floor with his fingernails broken and bloodied from clawing at the floorboards, whispering a name she did not know, begging forgiveness from a guest only he could see.

And beneath the willow tree, the grass grew greener still.

The dame was laid out on the linoleum like yesterday's news, the kind nobody bothers to recycle. Rain tapped at the window with the patience of a collection agent, and the smell in that room—Christ, the smell. Like the city itself had finally stopped pretending and shown me what it kept under its fingernails.

She'd been pretty once. You could still see it, the way you can still see the bones of a good neighborhood under twenty years of boarded windows and bad intentions. Somebody had gone to work on her with something ugly. Something with teeth. The blood had dried into the floorboards the way rust settles into the fire escapes along Kerrigan Street—permanent, like a debt you inherit.

I crouched down. My knees complained. Everything complains these days. The body had that gray cast to it, the color of snow three days after it falls in this town, when it's soaked up every exhaust pipe and broken promise the boulevard has to offer. Her lipstick was still on. Funny, the things that outlast us. Lipstick and parking tickets and the particular silence of a room where something terrible has happened.

Whoever did this knew her. You don't get this kind of mess from a stranger. Strangers are efficient—they're the wrecking ball. This was the slow kind of demolition, the kind that happens from the inside, one tenant at a time, until the whole building's just a facade waiting for a strong wind.

I lit a cigarette. Didn't help. Nothing helps. The city was already composting her in its memory, the way it composted the rest of us—grinding us down into the soil it would use to grow the next crop of suckers, the next batch of dreamers too stupid to stay out of the rain.

Somewhere a siren started up. Late, as usual. 

I started looking for what the killer left behind. They always leave something. This town's built on what people leave behind.

By the time she'd moved on, the drone had already logged the thermal signature, and the marker had gone out across the private channel.

Now she ran along the dry creek bed, and the stones tried to betray her feet.

She was forty-one. That was old for a Runner. Most didn't sign past thirty-five—couldn't—but Yuna had something the young ones lacked. She had a daughter in the Tiers who needed another six years of medication, and a contract that paid out on every sunrise she survived. She had reached the four-hundredth. Today was the thousandth mile of her lifetime in the Preserve.

Behind her, somewhere in the pines, a hunting horn sounded. They still used horns. The clients liked the theater of it.

---

Castellan Voss lowered the horn and smiled beneath his visor.

"She's making for the ravine," his guide murmured. "Old instinct. They always break for water."

"Let her." Voss slid the carbon-fiber crossbow from his shoulder rig. The weapon had cost more than most cities. "I want to see her face."

He had paid eleven million for this tag. Yuna Reyes, Runner 4471, holder of the longest active contract in the Northern Preserve. Legendary, in the circles that traded such legends. To take her would mean a plaque in the Lodge and whispered deference at every gala until he died.

He moved through the pines with the patience of a man who had never, in his life, been told to hurry.

---

She heard him before she saw him. Not footsteps—the *absence* of the small forest sounds, a pocket of silence moving closer.

Yuna stopped running.

She had always imagined, on the day it came, that she would keep running until the bolt took her in the back. That was the dignified way, the way the old Runners spoke about in the barracks. *Die facing forward.* But her legs simply would not carry her another step, and some deeper thing in her—older than dignity, older than fear—turned her around.

She sat down on a flat gray stone by the creek.

When Voss stepped out of the trees, he hesitated. Just for a moment. They were supposed to run. That was the point. A sitting Runner was like a painting that had climbed out of its frame.

"You're Reyes," he said.

"I know."

He approached slowly, crossbow lowered but not holstered. He was tall, gray at the temples, handsome in the expensive way that men become handsome when they have never had to be anything else.

"A thousand miles," he said. "That's quite a thing."

"It's a number."

"Will you stand? For the—" He gestured vaguely. "For the recording."

Yuna looked at him. Her thigh had stopped bleeding. A jay called once in the canopy and went silent.

"No," she said.

Voss nodded slowly, as if he had expected this, as if he were a connoisseur who had read of such refusals in the memoirs of older hunters. He raised the crossbow.

"My daughter's name is Mira," Yuna said, conversational. "She's fourteen. She likes—"

The bolt took her through the hollow of the throat. She had known it would; she had only wanted to say the name aloud one more time in the open air, where the trees might remember it, since he certainly would not.

---

Voss had the guide take the photograph.

He knelt behind the body, one gloved hand lifting her chin toward the lens, the other resting on the stock of the crossbow across his knee. The light through the pines was very fine. The guide took three shots to be sure.

"A good session, sir," the guide said.

"A good session," Voss agreed. He was already thinking about dinner.

Somewhere, in an apartment in the Tiers, a girl named Mira sat by a window and watched her screen for the sunrise notification that would not come.

The forest kept its silence. It had learned, long ago, that silence was the only thing it was permitted to keep.

# The Weight of Iron

The rain had been falling for three days when they came over the wire.

Thomas Ashford pressed himself against the sodden duckboards, his Lee-Enfield jammed with mud, useless as a crutch to a drowning man. The whistle had come too late. The flares had come too late. Everything in this war came too late except death, which always seemed to arrive on time.

He heard the German before he saw him—boots sliding in the muck, breath heaving through a throat raw from running. Thomas's hand found the trench shovel propped against the revetment. Standard issue. Sharpened along one edge by Corporal Blake three weeks ago, back when Blake still had a face.

The German rounded the traverse.

He was young. That was the first thing Thomas registered, in the split second before everything became motion. Young, with a dark mustache that hadn't fully come in, and eyes that went wide at the sight of him—wide with the same animal terror Thomas knew was mirrored in his own.

The German had a pistol. He was raising it.

Thomas swung.

The shovel took him across the jaw and the sound was not what Thomas expected. He had imagined, in the long nights of waiting, that violence would sound like the pictures—clean, theatrical. Instead there was a wet crack, like a boot breaking through ice into shallow water, and the German went sideways into the trench wall. The pistol fell. Thomas didn't see where.

He should have stopped. Later, for years, he would tell himself he should have stopped. The man was already down, already finished, perhaps. But Thomas's body had been wound tight for eleven months of shelling and rats and the screams of men calling for mothers in three languages, and something in him had come loose from its moorings.

He swung again. And again.

The second blow caught the German in the temple and something gave way beneath the metal—a softness that should not have been there, that no man should ever feel through the handle of a tool meant for digging. The third blow was unnecessary. The fourth was for Blake. The fifth was for his brother Edwin, buried somewhere near Loos. The sixth, he could not account for.

When he stopped, he was on his knees in the mud, and the mud was no longer only mud.

The rain kept falling.

Thomas sat back against the trench wall and looked at what he had done. The German's face was not a face anymore. His left hand was still twitching, the fingers curling and uncurling like a spider dying on a windowsill, and Thomas watched this small horror with a detachment that frightened him more than anything else. He thought: *I should feel something*. And then: *I am feeling something*. And then he could not name what it was.

In the dead man's breast pocket, visible where the tunic had torn open, was the corner of a photograph. Thomas did not look at it. He would not look at it. If he looked at it there would be a woman, or a child, or an old man standing stiffly beside a garden gate, and Thomas understood with a clarity sharper than any bayonet that if he saw that photograph he would not survive this war—not in any way that mattered.

He turned his face to the rain and let it wash what it could from his cheeks.

Someone was shouting down the line. English voices. The counter-attack had held. Men were alive who had not been alive a minute ago, and men were dead who had been living, and the arithmetic of it all was being tallied somewhere far away by people who would never smell what Thomas was smelling now—copper and shit and the strange sweetness of opened bone.

He became aware that he was still holding the shovel. His fingers would not release it. He had to pry them open one by one with his other hand, like unbending wire, and when the shovel finally fell it made no sound in the mud.

Private Haines came around the traverse, saw the German, saw Thomas, and said nothing. There was nothing to say. Haines had done his own killing that morning, and his eyes held that same flat light, the light of a lamp left burning in an empty room.

"You alright, Tommy?"

Thomas opened his mouth. He meant to say yes. He meant to say he was fine, that it was nothing, that he had only done what needed doing.

What came out was laughter—brief, wrong, the laughter of a man who has just understood a terrible joke—and then nothing at all.

He sat in the rain beside the body of the boy he had killed, and he understood that some part of him had gone into the mud with the German, and that no amount of digging with any shovel in the world would ever bring it back up.
